value.text: WPTV is bringing Let's Hear It to Martin County on Monday, Nov. 16, and we want to hear from you.Our team will be at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast, located at 1707 NE Indian River Dr., Jensen Beach, FL 34957, on Monday, Nov. to 6:30 p.m.We want to connect with you in person and hear about the stories that matter most to you. Whether you're dealing with a problem that needs answers or there's an issue affecting your community that deserves attention, we want to be your voice and help you find solutions.Can't make it on Nov. We still want to hear from you. While we hold monthly Let's Hear It meet-ups across our community, we know not everyone is able to attend in person.You can reach the WPTV Let's Hear It team anytime by emailing LetsHearIt@wptv.com.

A Fort Pierce woman is recovering from devastating flooding that destroyed her childhood home, marking the second time in two years she has lost everything. Terri Polk, who previously lost her home in the Spanish Lakes community to a tornado during Hurricane Milton, moved back into her childhood home to care for her mother, who has Alzheimer’s. Now, that home has been severely damaged by floodwaters. “The heart throb of our whole family is here,” Polk said. Polk shared that the house, built by her parents, has always been a central place for her family. “My mother’s door has always been open to everyone in the family,” she said. “This breaks your heart because I grew up in this house, I actually grew up here.” Last Monday, floodwaters rushed into the home, leaving behind destruction. “In the morning, the water was up to the tops of the beds,” Polk said. By the time the water receded, the damage was done. Polk’s belongings, including her bed and bookcases, now lie in a pile on the front lawn. Polk said she hasn’t slept in days as she tries to process the loss. The home is now filled with dehumidifiers, and Polk’s flood insurance won’t cover all the damages. Despite the challenges, she remains determined to rebuild. “No is not the answer; quit is not an option,” she said. “I’m not going to give up." A day after Jensen Beach residents told Martin County commissioners that flooding forced them from their homes, families can go to Hoke Library for recovery help while they wait for word on federal aid. The flood recovery center is open Wednesday even though regular library services are closed for Veterans Day. State agencies and local nonprofits are there to connect residents with recovery resources, and the county says more agencies and services will be added throughout the week. At Tuesday’s commission meeting, residents pressed county leaders about drainage and how they were warned. Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes and that assessment teams planned to visit each one to document the damage. Cleanup begins in Skyline Heights On Wednesday, CBS12 News returned to Jensen Beach’s Skyline Heights neighborhood, where part of Hyline Drive remained underwater. At Lisa French’s home, the cleanup had finally started. French said hers was the first home in the neighborhood being cleared out and gutted. Cabinets, furniture and pieces of drywall covered the front yard as workers carried out nearly everything floodwater touched. After a week, this is like celebration, French said. But that progress came with tears as she watched her family’s belongings get thrown away. The crib was a rough one to watch go, French said. It’s just my kids, you know. One week earlier, streets throughout the neighborhood were underwater and residents used kayaks to check on their homes and neighbors. Waite told CBS12 News that some homes took on three to five feet of water. She estimated about 24 of the 77 affected homes were destroyed. French and her family are staying with her parents and waiting to hear about longer-term housing. She said they do not have flood insurance. Alaura Macpherson, co-founder of Quit Messing With Jensen, went to the Hoke Library resource center Wednesday to collect cleanup supplies for affected families. CBS12 News later met up with her at French’s home, where she was helping the family clear out the damage. Absolutely not, Macpherson said. I will do this any day for my community. For French, getting everything out is only the beginning. This is bittersweet because we’re moving forward, French said. But, you know, how do we rebuild? Where to get help The Multi-Agency Resource Center is at Hoke Library, 1150 NW Jack Williams Way in Jensen Beach . The county lists those hours for Wednesday through Saturday until further notice. The center is closed Sundays. Martin County is also accepting applications for state disaster housing assistance. Households must meet income requirements. Residents can call 772-320-3169 for details. They can also report flood damage and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Read more: 'We're not getting any answers': Hamilton Bay residents frustrated as flooding continues Where FEMA aid stands Florida announced Monday that it had requested a presidential major disaster declaration for the flooding. As of Wednesday morning, federal approval had yet to be announced. The state’s announcement did not specify whether the request included FEMA Individual Assistance for Martin County. If that aid is authorized for Martin County, eligible households could apply for help with expenses such as temporary housing and essential home repairs.

More than a week after historic rainfall hit the Treasure Coast, Martin County leaders are looking at how to prevent another flooding disaster after officials said Port St. Lucie pumped floodwater into the Savannas Preserve before water flowed south toward neighborhoods in Jensen Beach.WATCH REPORT BELOW:The flooding and damage came days after the historic rainfall stopped, leaving residents questioning what happened, who was pumping water into the preserve and what can be changed before another major storm.WPTV's Michael Hoffman has been following those questions as families continue recovering from homes that were damaged or destroyed.Residents have told WPTV they believe pumping floodwater from areas to the north contributed to the natural flow of water moving south and overflowing into their Jensen Beach neighborhoods.Tiffany Kincaid was among the residents whose homes were devastated.“I've never seen anything like this, not this level of devastation that has been sort of sitting in water for now eight days,” Kincaid said.Kincaid said her family believed protections were in place until rising water forced them out."We trusted that a plan was in place to protect us, until midnight when water became entering our home, and then we quickly realized that we needed to get out," Kincaid said.At a Martin County Commission meeting, Public Works Director James Gorton acknowledged the challenge presented by the historic rainfall."The severity of that rainfall caught us unprepared," Gorton said. It caught Indian River unprepared."Gorton also addressed pumping from Port St. Lucie into the Savannas Preserve."They pumped Monday and they pumped Tuesday morning. They stopped Tuesday morning," Gorton said.Gorton said one concern is that individual jurisdictions may be looking primarily at conditions within their own watersheds rather than what happens farther downstream."They're just looking at the water levels that are in their watershed," Gorton said. "They're not looking at their impacts to the downstream."The pumping itself is not an illegal practice. Lucie has a permit allowing it to pump into the preserve, and Martin County leaders said there are not concrete regulation schedules governing the Savannas as a whole.That has raised a bigger question for local leaders: Who should be responsible for considering the consequences across the entire watershed?“I don't know that we can modify their permit, but I would hope that we'd be able to look at that and say, you know, do no harm, which is really what kind of — or shared adversity, I think, is a better way to say it,” Gorton said.One potential solution discussed by Martin County officials would put management of the Savannas watershed under one overarching organization rather than relying on decisions made by individual jurisdictions.“Once we get that water out, there's a larger discussion that we need to have, which is: What are we going to do to mitigate this in the future?” Gorton said.He suggested the water management district could potentially play a role."One such idea might be looking at treating the Savannas as a watershed that needs to be managed by one party," Gorton said. "Maybe it would be the water management district."Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi agreed that the current situation warrants another look."I agree with what your suggestion was, is that it just can't be whoever pumps fastest and first wins," Ciampi said.For people still dealing with the consequences in Jensen Beach, those discussions come as they search for answers, assistance and, in some cases, a dry place to call home.WPTV will continue following whether Martin County and other agencies develop a new plan for managing water in the Savannas and what changes could be made before another major rainfall event.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County family is searching for answers after 18-year-old Omari Linzell Williams was struck and killed by a vehicle while walking to get groceries. His family told WPTV they are now calling for changes to make the roadway safer for pedestrians as the traffic homicide investigation continues.Williams' mother, Witney Williams, and aunt, Sharon Garcia, spoke with WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache about the loss and the questions they still have about what happened."He was pure, he was a beautiful, beautiful young man. He was a big brother," Witney Williams said.WATCH REPORT BELOW:Omari Linzell Williams was walking to get groceriesInvestigators said Williams was walking along the westbound lane of North Boulevard around 6 p.m. Tuesday when a 30-year-old driver struck him.According to investigators, the driver was unable to see Williams before the collision. Mary's Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead.The driver was not injured and cooperated with investigators.Williams' family told WPTV he had left home to pick up groceries because the family did not have a vehicle."There was floodwaters on the opposite side of the road so he couldn't walk on that side," Garcia said."At this moment they don't have a car and he was walking to the store to get the items and he didn't make it very far," she said.His mother says she knew something was wrongWitney Williams said she became concerned after seeing a social media post and being unable to reach her son by phone."I ran out of the house screaming my son's name because I knew that was him," she said.Williams said she rushed toward the scene, hoping she would get there in time."I was just praying that I'd get there before he took his last breath and I didn't make it," she said.The family is now seeking more information about the circumstances surrounding the crash."We miss him and we just want answers," Garcia said. "We just want to know like any family, what happened."Family remembers Omari as a big brother who helped othersAs they grieve, Williams' relatives want people to remember more than the circumstances of his death.His mother described him as an involved and caring older brother to his six siblings, who regularly stepped in when she needed help."Anything I needed, he would always be the one, 'Well, I can do it for you, Mom,'" she said.After his death, the family said people began reaching out to share stories about how Williams had helped them through difficult periods in their lives."They reach out to us after the accident to let us know how amazing Omari was and how he saved lives," his mother said.Williams' family said they learned he had used an online platform to connect with and support people who were struggling. His mother said one person told them Williams had helped save an older man from taking his own life.Family calls for sidewalks, lights and other safety changesWilliams' family is now pushing for pedestrian safety improvements in the area where he was killed."I want answers and things need to be done to put in place for other children because this is going to happen to somebody else's child," his mother said."We need sidewalks, we need speed bumps and we need lights," she added.Garcia said the family also plans to launch a petition in Williams' name aimed at making the roadway safer."We're gonna have a petition in Omari's name to try to make that road a safer road," she said.Williams' mother said turning her grief into action has become part of her mission."It sucks that I lost mine, but I'm going to fight to make sure this doesn't happen to another kid," she said.The traffic homicide investigation remains ongoing.Candlelight vigil planned for OmariWilliams' family plans to hold a candlelight vigil in his memory at 6 p.m. Friday at Lakewood Park in the Fort Pierce area.The gathering will give relatives, friends and members of the community an opportunity to remember the 18-year-old whose family says was devoted to his siblings and helping others.The family also started a fundraiser to help ease funeral expenses. Lucie County animal shelter is making an urgent push to find homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month.The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency "Empty the Shelters" adoption event on Nov. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event.The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home in October.The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges.Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals.All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped.The event runs from 11 a.m. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Lucie.Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org.

As garlands, ornaments, lights and ribbons begin marking the start of another holiday season, Donte Bates is thinking about families who may have a harder time celebrating.Bates is the co-founder and executive director of Love, Hope & Healing Inc., a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit focused on at-risk, underserved and underrepresented youth and families. The organization says its work centers on wellness, mental health support, mentorship and life skills.WATCH REPORT BELOW: For Bates, the name captures what he believes people need most."We all need love. We're all looking for hope, and we all need healing," Bates said. "And we, as we know, the world, the whole world needs healing right now."That mission takes on added meaning during the holidays, when Bates says he sees families struggling to afford some of the thing that make the season special."Families that's going through these hardships, and now you're coming up to Christmas time when it's supposed to be the happy time festive, and they don't have nothing to eat," Bates said. "The kids can't get the toys that they're looking for. You just can't have some of the things that you actually grew up as a kid loving and looking to wake up to. A lot of parents and a lot of families are not getting it right now."Bates expects that need to grow."I'm pretty sure we're gonna have a lot more people coming and needing the help, and we're already seeing it before we even get to these holiday times of more people needing these resources," he said. "So I'm expecting it to be a huge number this year."For Bates, keeping young people on the right path is personal."I had to go away for two years because I wanted to live the street life, and so I feel like I gave away two years of my life so I could come back and help the kids behind me, not make the mistakes I made and don't go down that road," Bates said. "So the passion behind that is, hey, stay out of the system, stay out of the judicial system, stay out of the cemetery. I want you to be free, and I want them to succeed in life."The nonprofit's website says Bates and fellow founder Yolanda Bates both grew up in underserved communities. Their experiences helped create a desire to help other families address childhood trauma and generational challenges. Family, unity, education, empowerment and accountability are among the values the organization lists as central to its work.That work extends well beyond the holidays.Love, Hope & Healing Inc. has partnered with Palm Beach State College on summer programming that exposes high school students to skilled trades, careers and personal development. It has also offered entrepreneurship programming for young men ages 14 to 18.But Bates says helping children also means supporting the families they go home to."We mainly deal with the young, young men and women, but we can't deal with the young men and women and send them back into a toxic environment," Bates said. "So we actually tackle the parents as well."He describes that work as an effort to rebuild a support network around those families."Our kids definitely need it. Families need it as a whole. We're trying to recreate, no, not recreate, reestablish the village," Bates said. "They all, everybody says it takes a village. We want to reestablish and put a stronghold on that village."That village now includes volunteers like Christopher Hepburn, CEO and co-founder of a West Palm Beach branding and marketing agency.Hepburn said he has only been volunteering with the nonprofit for a few months, but its focus on bringing families together connected with his own childhood."Wow, it's really the families," Hepburn said. "When I grew up, I didn't really spend some time with my mom and my dad, so to see them putting that together for the families and the kids and seeing everyone come together, that's amazing to me. So yeah, it means everything."Hepburn has volunteered at events including a father-son grill challenge. Seeing fathers and sons spending time together was especially meaningful to him."Oh man, it was amazing," Hepburn said. "Yeah, I didn't really, like I said, I didn't spend that much time with my dad growing up, so to see fathers and sons get together and really just connect and, you know, just love each other, is, it's dope."For him, the idea behind a Season of Hope can be as simple as making time for one another."That just means to me just getting together as a family, talking with each other and really just connecting," Hepburn said.And he hopes the nonprofit's reach continues growing."I hope that it keeps going. I hope that the events get even bigger, get even better," Hepburn said. "I hope that more families get impacted and that it just spreads as fast as it can."Love, Hope & Healing Inc. is collaborating with United Way of Palm Beach Countysomething Bates believes can broaden the impact organizations have when they work together."That's been wonderful with the help we've been getting from United Way and actually coming up under their umbrella now. Every step of the way, they've been so helpful. Anytime you call, they're there to pick up the phone. So it's just been amazing, with just the love they've given our organization and seeing what we're doing in the community and willing to help," said Bates.The nonprofit is currently seeking volunteers and accepts donations to support its work in the community."We're looking for donations. We're looking for volunteers. We're looking for mentors," Bates said. "We're just looking for somebody to get behind us and have a collective impact because is the answer because the kids need it."And as the holidays approach, Bates has a simple message for families who may be struggling."Stay positive," Bates said. "Keep hope alive because help is on the way. We're out here doing it, and we know it's tough, but let's keep pushing through and let's get these resources to them."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Delray Beach Mayor Tom Carney says he's exploring a private-sector solution to keep the city's 2027 St. Patrick's Day Parade alive after a new Florida law prompted the city to announce it would cancel the event.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: The city's annual Pride Festival is also affected by the decision, which Carney says stems from Senate Bill 1134.The legislation restricts local governments from funding, promoting or taking official actions related to certain diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) activities.Carney said the potential impact on the two events has been top of mind since the bill passed."We learned very quickly that, within the scope of the definition of DEI, it could (impact both) the St. Patrick's Day parade and the Pride festival," Carney said.After the city announced the cancellation, Carney said residents quickly voiced their concerns."I would say by Saturday I had a good 50 emails in my box saying, 'What are you doing?'" he said.Now, the mayor is looking at another option: allowing private organizers and sponsors to take the lead.Carney said the St. Patrick's Day parade used to be a private event and his family also participated in underwriting it in the past. He said he's already reached out to potential supporters, and others have contacted him offering to help fund the parade."I decided, well, let's just make it a private event again, so I reached out to a half dozen people. More than that reached out to me saying, 'We'll help underwrite the parade,' and we've already got people submitting applications to try and do the parade for us," Carney said.The mayor said a similar arrangement could be considered for the Pride Festival."If the private sector wants to support that, I would as well," Carney said. "You don't want to cancel things people have grown accustomed to."Residents said losing either event would have an impact beyond the festivities themselves, including on the local business community and residents who look forward to celebrating their traditions.Carney says discussions are still in the early stages, but he's confident the St. Patrick's Day Parade will go on as scheduled in 2027.The city has not yet announced a finalized plan for either event.Senate Bill 1143 takes effect Jan.

Democrat Scott Colom is projected to defeat Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's U.S. Senate race, according to the Associated Press, pulling off a major upset in a state that has long favored Republicans.Colom's victory makes him the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since 1982. The state has not had a Democratic senator since John Stennis left office in 1989.WATCH: A new generation on Capitol Hill could challenge Chuck Schumer's Senate leadershipThe race was not initially considered competitive, but polling tightened in the closing weeks of the campaign as voters expressed growing frustration with the economy.Hyde-Smith faced criticism after suggesting during an interview that consumers could choose other sources of protein when asked about rising beef prices.Colom seized on the remark, launching a campaign ad featuring voters who said they would rather choose another senator than another protein.The race also drew attention from national political figures. President Donald Trump visited Mississippi a week before Election Day to rally support for Hyde-Smith, while former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned for Colom in the closing weeks of the race.Colom's victory delivers Democrats an unexpected pickup in the U.S.

If the 2026 midterms were an opportunity for voters to express their feelings about President Donald Trump’s administration, the election in two years will be their first opportunity to cast a vote for president without his name on the ballot.Trump is constitutionally barred from running again, which means, as the lame duck portion of his presidency comes into view, it’s not too early to start thinking about who might replace him.Potential candidates certainly are. While they might bat away speculation, many are starting to think seriously about their potential path or wrestling with the ultimate question — is it worth the investment of time and energy and the guarantee of being vilified by your political rivals in the off chance that you could be the most powerful person in the world?RELATED STORY | Kamala Harris returns to campaign trail as 2028 speculation growsA little more than half of Americans, 54%, have given at least some thought to the coming presidential race, according to a CNN Poll conducted by SSRS in the month before the midterm election. Fewer, 40%, said they’re looking forward to it, with 27% saying they’re dreading it and the rest expressing neither outlook.No major candidate has yet declared a campaign, although the first of those could come sooner than many people think.Most Americans don’t yet have a 2028 candidate in mindAbout a third of Americans, 35%, said there’s a specific candidate they’d like to see run, compared to 64% who are taking more of a wait-and-see attitude.The two Republican politicians whose names were most frequently mentioned were Secretary of State Marco Rubio, at 8%, and Vice President JD Vance at 7%. President Donald Trump has joked about the two men being rivals or even forming a ticket together. Rubio has said he would defer to Vance.Among Democratic politicians, California Gov. Gavin Newsom (3%), former Vice President and Democrats’ 2024 nominee Kamala Harris (2%), and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg (2%) were the only potential candidates to get the attention of more than 1% of Americans in the poll.Things changed when Americans were asked by pollsters about specific candidates.Harris is the most known DemocratAbout a quarter of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents said they would be excited to support Harris (27%), Rep, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (27%), and Buttigieg (26%). Slightly fewer (22%) said they would be excited to support Newsom or Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona and 16% expressed excitement about Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia.The poll was conducted before the midterms, however, and Ossoff has clearly generated some buzz. He won the straw poll at a conference for Democratic activists, Crooked Con, held the weekend after Ossoff’s commanding reelection in Georgia. He has said he has no interest in running for president.Harris has the most total support. More than three-quarters of Democrats and Democratic leaners (51%) said that they would at least consider backing her. But she is also the most well-known of the candidates. Just 7% said they didn’t know enough about her to offer an opinion, compared with 55% who said the same of Ossoff. Harris also had the highest portion of Democratic-aligned adults, 15%, who said they would never support her.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Potential 2028 Democratic contenders set to discuss party’s future at post-midterms meetingMore than 60% said they didn’t know enough about some other potential candidates, including Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, all of whom have been mentioned as potential candidates.Midterms could also have buoyed someone like Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who handily won reelection and also helped flip multiple house seats to Democrats in his swing state. In CNN’s poll, just 10% said they’d be excited to support him, 28% said they’d consider it, and 54% said they didn’t have enough information.Vance and Rubio generate excitementVance and Rubio get similar marks from Republicans and Republican leaners: 41% said they would be excited to support Vance and 41% said they would be excited to support Rubio. Vance, however, may have a wider pool of potential support, with 77% of GOP-aligned adults saying they’d at least consider supporting him, compared with 65% who said the same of Rubio.The midterms could affect those numbers. Vance has sought some distance from Trump on the issue of the Iran war, which he blames for Republican losses. While as Vice President, Vance has largely been viewed as Trump’s heir apparent, in a post-election interview with CBS News, Trump said he might not support anyone in the coming Republican primary.“Maybe I’m better off not getting involved,” Trump said.There are a number of potential candidates who generate opposition on the GOP side. Nearly half of Republicans or Republican-leaners, 46%, said they would never support former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie and 30% said they would never support former South Carolina Gov. Both Christie and Haley have been critics of Trump and run against him in previous primaries. A substantial block also said they would not support Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth (25%), HHS Secretary Robert F. Rand Paul of Kentucky (24%).It’s early, but also…The election is a little less than two years away. So while it’s worth looking at the potential field, it’s also worth acknowledging that things could change.In 2014, two years before Trump went on to win the White House for the first time he wasn’t included when CNN asked Americans about potential candidates. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, however, was the top listed Democrat. She would go on to get the nomination.In 2018, two years before Joe Biden went on to become president, he had the most support among Democrats but was far short of a majority.In 2022, two years before Trump won reelection, a slim majority of Republicans and Republican leaners wanted someone who wasn’t named Trump. He ended up with the nomination and the White House.But the Trump era is coming to an end, and the coming presidential election will be the most open on both sides of the political aisle since 2008.The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros.

Veterans of all eras and residents of all ages packed Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday for the annual Veterans Day ceremony.WPTV anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with fellow veterans about the significance of the day.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service "It's all like my whole history. I started in transportation. I think it's very important. I enlisted and was not supposed to go but ended up over there," Greene told Trim.Wayne Thomas, another Vietnam War veteran in attendance, told Trim he felt this day now properly honors their service, which was not previously recognized."It's good to get the recognition that we didn't get," Thomas said.The Port St. Lucie High School Junior ROTC attended the ceremony in full force while crowds of all ages looked on.That included a member of the greatest generation: 98-year-old World War II veteran Robert Vogel."I'm one of the few left. I would really encourage anyone to come to these events because they're really important to support the veterans," Vogel told Trim.Those veterans heard keynote speaker, Retired Air Force Master Sgt. Vincent Lavelle Jr.A special touch from the Port St. Lucie community band featured songs from each branch of service.That prompted service members in attendance to stand for their respective branch song.There was also a special flyover by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office helicopter.

MARTY public transportation is beginning a phased return in Martin County after more than a month without regular bus service, starting with ADA paratransit before service expands to the U.S. Highway 1 and Indiantown routes, according to the county.WATCH: MARTY bus service begins returning in Martin CountyThe restoration will not happen all at once. Martin County said additional service will be added as buses are prepared and drivers become available. The county has not announced a date for full MARTY service to return.For riders who rely on public transportation to get to work, buy groceries or reach medical appointments, the phased restart offers some relief after weeks of limited transportation options.MARTY riders were left scrambling Oct. 8 when the county's transit provider abruptly stopped service.One rider, Joe, told WPTV at the time that he received no warning."No warning at all. Zero," Joe said.For him, losing bus service was more than an inconvenience. He told WPTV that injuries limited his mobility and made finding another way to get around difficult."I've had two broken necks, three broken backs. Lucie County animal shelter is making an urgent push to find homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency "Empty the Shelters" adoption event on Nov. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

Following a brief pause, the Martin County Board of Commissioners announced on Tuesday that the county has reached a resolution to begin phased restoration of MARTY transit services. The county says it has reached a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit, LLC to begin the phased restoration of public transportation services following an abrupt disruption due to a contract breach by the prior vendor. Last month, MARTY public transit services in Martin County abruptly stopped after its operator withdrew from its contract due to rising operating costs. This left many people without a regular bus service. The county now says it will be taking a phased approach to resuming operations, prioritizing riders who rely on ADA paratransit services, then working towards restoring fixed-route services. See also: Delray Beach says new Florida law will block St. Patrick’s Day, Pride events For those who with disabilities who cannot use regular fixed-route bus services, ADA paratransit services are expected to resume on Thursday, Nov. Details regarding scheduling and reservations are available at 772-463-2822 , the county says. A start date for restoration of full services has yet to be announced. Our priority is to restore public transportation as quickly and responsibly as possible, with particular attention to residents who depend on these services to access essential needs, as well as fiscal responsibility to the taxpayer, said Ash Beecher, Martin County Transit Administrator. We recognize the disruption this has caused for our riders and the broader community, and we are working to reestablish service in a thoughtful, coordinated manner.

Beds will be rolling down Flagler Avenue in Stuart as Family Promise of Martin County brings its annual Bed Races back to Sailfish Ballpark, turning an unusual competition into a community effort to help families with children facing homelessness. The free event is scheduled for Saturday from 10 a.m. at Sailfish Ballpark, 600 SE Flagler Ave. Teams turn beds into racing machines, with runners pushing a rider toward the finish line. But behind the costumes, competition and laughs are a serious mission. Madeleine Bozone Greenwood, executive director of Family Promise of Martin County, said the organization works to prevent and end family homelessness in Martin County. "We serve parents with children that are here in Martin County," Greenwood said. "We provide shelter, transitional housing. A path to return to home ownership or their own rental housing." Pastor Chad Fair, board chair of Family Promise of Martin County, said homelessness does not always look the way people might expect. "We kind of think that it hits just those people we see on the street corner, but it's families, it's nurses, it's school teachers, it's people that are integral in our community and do the work with our kids, with our families, and they're experiencing homelessness," Fair said. Family Promise says its work includes homelessness prevention, shelter and services designed to help families find stable housing while keeping parents and children together. That work gives the bed races a literal connection to the organization's mission: The race may be entertaining, but the bed represents something every family needs at the end of the day, a safe place to sleep. Paige Cortes, director of operations for Family Promise of Martin County, said spectators can attend Saturday's event for free . "This Saturday, bed races 10 to 1 at the Sailfish Ballpark," Cortes said. "So we are ready for fun too, and you can join us in the race to end childhood homelessness." The event combines the spectacle of beds on wheels with the broader goal of connecting Martin County residents with an issue that can sometimes remain largely invisible. For working families facing a housing crisis, Fair said homelessness can affect people who are already contributing to the community every day. That gives Saturday's race a purpose beyond deciding which team can push its bed across the finish line fastest. It gives residents an opportunity to learn about family homelessness in Martin County and the organizations working to help families regain stable housing. Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

Learning to navigate without relying on sight requires skills many people may never have considered, from using a white cane to technology that reads or magnifies what's on a computer screen.At Lighthouse for the Blind of the Palm Beaches, Treasure Coast & Okeechobee in West Palm Beach, those tools are helping people who are blind or visually impaired build greater independence.The organization serves people ranging from babies to seniors across five counties, executive director Lisa Stella told WPTV.For children, that can include activities designed to be sensory-oriented and inclusive in the community.One of the skills taught at the Lighthouse is how to use a white cane to navigate an environment.During WPTV's visit, Shining A Light reporter T.A. Walker put on a blindfold and attempted a mobility exercise with Elizabeth Prus, Lighthouse for the Blind's youth services director.Prus instructed Walker to sweep the cane back and forth roughly the width of his shoulders as he walked. The cane provided information about objects in his path, including a chair and a kitchen island."This is a tool that people who are visually impaired use to navigate environments," Prus said.The training can begin at a young age."We start with little kids, teaching them how to use a cane so that way they can travel independently," Prus said.For Walker, temporarily navigating without sight offered a firsthand look at how a white cane can provide information about the environment around him.The Lighthouse also helps clients use technology designed to make computers more accessible to people who are blind or have low vision.Brandon Butzberger demonstrated ZoomText Fusion, software he uses on a computer."It's called ZoomText Fusion," Butzberger said. "It's a software that has the screen reading (narration) capabilities that Tekesha is showing, as well as magnification."Tekesha Saffold also demonstrated audio software she uses to navigate her computer.Both Butzberger and Saffold are former Lighthouse clients who later became employees, turning their own experiences with the organization into an opportunity to help others.That full-circle journey provides another example of what independence can look like.Butzberger is now an adjustment to blindness counselor at the Lighthouse, while Saffold works as an intake specialist.Their experiences show how skills and resources designed to increase independence can carry beyond a classroom or training session and into education, employment and everyday life.The Lighthouse's work spans generations. Stella said the organization serves people from babies through seniors across Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie, Indian River and Okeechobee counties.Mobility training is one piece of that work. Assistive technology provides another.Together, the demonstrations at the West Palm Beach Lighthouse offered a look at how people who are blind or visually impaired can use training, technology and practical tools to navigate their surroundings and perform everyday tasks independently.For some former clients, the journey has come full circle. After receiving services themselves, they're now working at the Lighthouse and helping others develop skills of their own.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Treasure Coast woman who lost her home two years ago to a tornado from Hurricane Milton has lost another home to devastating flooding in Fort Pierce."I'm starting to feel like I'm invincible at this point," says Terry Polk as she watched the debris pile of drywall and ruined furniture in front of her home get bigger.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The water in her home was measured in feet, not inches, as the heavy rain in the first weekend of November flooded her block."We were actually in the house," Polk said. The King's Academy volleyball team brought home the school's first championship in 20 years, defeating the Pine Crest Panthers on Nov. Many businesses are reeling in the effects of last week’s historic flooding event across South Florida, including a local Vero Beach citrus grove farm. CBS12 News Photojournalist Chris Pollock visited Greene Sugars Farm in Vero Beach, a family-owned farm business that spans multiple generations. The farm has been amongst the hardest hit from the historic flooding. Aubrey Greene shared with CBS12 News that they had a great citrus season last year, and were anticipating another good year this year, that was until the flooding put their crops, trees, and livestock in jeopardy. Greene Sugars boasts 800 acres of lemon trees, 50 acres of sugar belle trees, and 1000’s of cattle. They put out roughly 60,000-80,000 boxes of citrus per year and have a contract with Coca-Cola. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium Greene shared that the farm was hit with over 10 inches of rain in one single night, and that the citrus groves have been flooded trunk to trunk in water for over a week, despite heavy pumping every morning and night. That amount of rain over all of this land, it’s crazy, Greene said.

Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Palm Beach is balancing four community efforts this week, from responding to people displaced by a plane crash and flooding to opening an interactive museum designed to help people better understand poverty.Ellen T. Wayne, CEO of Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Palm Beach, said the organization has been working with people affected by two emergencies while preparing to welcome the public to the People of Hope Mobile Museum and its “Spare Change, Share Hope” campaign.WATCH REPORT BELOW: “We got hit with a double whammy,” Wayne said. “First, we're responding to the individuals who have been displaced as a result of the plane crash here in Palm Beach County, and then, now we're in full disaster response mode working with individuals who've been impacted by this [recent] flooding that we've had across our five counties in our diocese.”The first two efforts involve Catholic Charities' response to immediate needs in the community.Wayne said the organization has been assisting people displaced by the Palm Beach County plane crash.At the same time, Catholic Charities has moved into disaster response following flooding across the five-county area served by the Diocese of Palm Beach (Okeechobee, Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Palm Beach counties).Those efforts are an extension of the organization's everyday work with people experiencing vulnerable situations, Wayne said.The third effort brings a different kind of assistance to the community: understanding.The People of Hope Mobile Museum is a traveling interactive museum housed inside an expandable semi-truck. It is visiting Catholic Charities agencies across the United States and is making a stop at the Cathedral of St. Ignatius Loyola in Palm Beach Gardens.Wayne said the experience is intended to give visitors a glimpse into the lives of people dealing with poverty while sharing stories of resilience, perseverance, and hope.Visitors can experience an interactive simulator that explores situations faced by people living in poverty, record their own stories, and leave messages of hope for others.The museum also explores circumstances faced by seniors, people experiencing homelessness, and other people Catholic Charities serves.“Oftentimes, people, when they're hearing a story of an individual struggling, will think, ‘Well, why did they do that or why didn't they do something else?’” Wayne said. “This is really going to give our guests an opportunity to see the challenges and the decisions that people have to make every day and the reality that there's no easy way out.”The pop-up museum is free to attend Friday and Saturday.The fourth effort happening this weekend is the "Spare Change. Share Hope." campaign.Visitors who want to support Catholic Charities can contribute through a QR code associated with the campaign.The campaign complements the museum's larger message by giving visitors an opportunity to move from learning about challenges their neighbors face to helping people in need.Wayne described that connection by saying Catholic Charities has “people out in the field doing the work of Hope,” while the museum gives others an opportunity to learn what it means to become a person of hope themselves.The timing gives the People of Hope Museum added relevance in Palm Beach County.While Catholic Charities responds to people affected by emergencies, the museum asks visitors to consider the difficult decisions people can face when circumstances suddenly change.“It's always easier to be on the outside looking in,” Wayne said. “This is intended to kind of open our eyes to what the struggles of people who are impoverished all across our country are facing.”The People of Hope Mobile Museum is at the Cathedral of St. Military Trail in Palm Beach Gardens.It is open Friday from 8:30 a.m. and Saturday from 8:30 a.m. Admission is free.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Palm Beach County students are helping scientists answer a deceptively simple question: Where does our trash go once it starts floating through local waterways?ANGARI Foundation plans to release bright orange, eco-friendly drift cards into the water on Nov. 10 at noon as part of its Lagoon Drift Card Study. Members of the public are then being asked to find the cards and report where they ended up.“So we're basically trying to track our trash,” Laura Jessop with ANGARI Foundation told WPTV. “So we put these eco-friendly drift cards in the water. They're going in on November 10 at 12 p.m., and we need the public to go out and find them.”The idea is to use the cards as stand-ins for other objects floating on the surface.“Everything that floats on the surface, that's what we're sort of tracking right now,” Jessop said.Each card found by a member of the public becomes another piece of information for the study.Jessop said knowing where the cards eventually turn up can help researchers identify places where floating debris could be accumulating.“They're bright orange, and if they report them to us, we can then look at where our trash is accumulating and really target those areas,” she said.The project involves Manatee Lagoon, where some of the drift cards will be released.Rachel Shanker with Manatee Lagoon said participating in the project can provide information that may ultimately help protect Florida's environment.“Here at Manatee Lagoon, we're so excited to be a part of this study where we can collect data and learn how to better preserve and protect Florida's environment and wildlife for future generations,” Shanker said.The study isn't limited to scientists and environmental organizations.Students from Palm Springs Community Middle School are creating their own drift cards and will release them at Manatee Lagoon on Nov. 10.A teacher participating in the project told WPTV the experiment gives students the opportunity to connect what they're studying in class with an actual environmental project.“My students are creating drift cards which they will be releasing on November 10 here at Manatee Lagoon, and they are doing this to track the pollution in the waterways and apply what we're learning in the classroom to the real world,” she said.And the students aren't sending anonymous pieces of orange material into the water.They're making the cards their own.One student decorated a card with water, a sun and a shark, before adding a marine-themed message: “You're 'fintastic.'”Another decorated a card as an ocean scene with a simple message for whoever eventually discovers it: “Love your ocean.”For students, the cards turn an environmental lesson into something tangible.They create the cards, release them, and wait to see where currents carry them. If members of the public find and report their locations, those discoveries become part of the study.That provides a real-world demonstration of something that can otherwise be difficult to visualize in a classroom: What happens to floating material after it enters a waterway?For the broader community, it also turns a walk along the water into an opportunity to participate in local science.If you spot one of the bright orange drift cards, it may be more than something that washed ashore. Its location is precisely the information researchers are looking for.The experiment comes just before another important date for the Lake Worth Lagoon.Manatee season officially begins Nov. 15.Shanker said cooler temperatures help bring manatees back toward Manatee Lagoon.“As the water temperatures drop, they start coming here to Manatee Lagoon for our warm water outflow,” Shanker said.Manatee Lagoon plans to celebrate the beginning of the season with a kickoff event Nov. 21.For the students creating drift cards, meanwhile, the next milestone comes Nov. 10, when their colorful creations leave their hands and begin their journey through South Florida's waterways.Where they end up is part of the experiment.Who finds them could be anyone.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A day after Jensen Beach residents told Martin County commissioners that flooding forced them from their homes, families can go to Hoke Library for recovery help while they wait for word on federal aid. The flood recovery center is open Wednesday even though regular library services are closed for Veterans Day. State agencies and local nonprofits are there to connect residents with recovery resources, and the county says more agencies and services will be added throughout the week. At Tuesday’s commission meeting, residents pressed county leaders about drainage and how they were warned. Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes and that assessment teams planned to visit each one to document the damage. Cleanup begins in Skyline Heights On Wednesday, CBS12 News returned to Jensen Beach’s Skyline Heights neighborhood, where part of Hyline Drive remained underwater. At Lisa French’s home, the cleanup had finally started. French said hers was the first home in the neighborhood being cleared out and gutted. Cabinets, furniture and pieces of drywall covered the front yard as workers carried out nearly everything floodwater touched. After a week, this is like celebration, French said. But that progress came with tears as she watched her family’s belongings get thrown away. The crib was a rough one to watch go, French said. It’s just my kids, you know. One week earlier, streets throughout the neighborhood were underwater and residents used kayaks to check on their homes and neighbors. Waite told CBS12 News that some homes took on three to five feet of water. She estimated about 24 of the 77 affected homes were destroyed. French and her family are staying with her parents and waiting to hear about longer-term housing. She said they do not have flood insurance. Alaura Macpherson, co-founder of Quit Messing With Jensen, went to the Hoke Library resource center Wednesday to collect cleanup supplies for affected families. CBS12 News later met up with her at French’s home, where she was helping the family clear out the damage. Absolutely not, Macpherson said. I will do this any day for my community. For French, getting everything out is only the beginning. This is bittersweet because we’re moving forward, French said. But, you know, how do we rebuild? Where to get help The Multi-Agency Resource Center is at Hoke Library, 1150 NW Jack Williams Way in Jensen Beach . The county lists those hours for Wednesday through Saturday until further notice. The center is closed Sundays. Martin County is also accepting applications for state disaster housing assistance. Households must meet income requirements. Residents can call 772-320-3169 for details. They can also report flood damage and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Read more: 'We're not getting any answers': Hamilton Bay residents frustrated as flooding continues Where FEMA aid stands Florida announced Monday that it had requested a presidential major disaster declaration for the flooding. As of Wednesday morning, federal approval had yet to be announced. The state’s announcement did not specify whether the request included FEMA Individual Assistance for Martin County. If that aid is authorized for Martin County, eligible households could apply for help with expenses such as temporary housing and essential home repairs.

More than a week after historic rainfall hit the Treasure Coast, Martin County leaders are looking at how to prevent another flooding disaster after officials said Port St. Lucie pumped floodwater into the Savannas Preserve before water flowed south toward neighborhoods in Jensen Beach.WATCH REPORT BELOW:The flooding and damage came days after the historic rainfall stopped, leaving residents questioning what happened, who was pumping water into the preserve and what can be changed before another major storm.WPTV's Michael Hoffman has been following those questions as families continue recovering from homes that were damaged or destroyed.Residents have told WPTV they believe pumping floodwater from areas to the north contributed to the natural flow of water moving south and overflowing into their Jensen Beach neighborhoods.Tiffany Kincaid was among the residents whose homes were devastated.“I've never seen anything like this, not this level of devastation that has been sort of sitting in water for now eight days,” Kincaid said.Kincaid said her family believed protections were in place until rising water forced them out."We trusted that a plan was in place to protect us, until midnight when water became entering our home, and then we quickly realized that we needed to get out," Kincaid said.At a Martin County Commission meeting, Public Works Director James Gorton acknowledged the challenge presented by the historic rainfall."The severity of that rainfall caught us unprepared," Gorton said. It caught Indian River unprepared."Gorton also addressed pumping from Port St. Lucie into the Savannas Preserve."They pumped Monday and they pumped Tuesday morning. They stopped Tuesday morning," Gorton said.Gorton said one concern is that individual jurisdictions may be looking primarily at conditions within their own watersheds rather than what happens farther downstream."They're just looking at the water levels that are in their watershed," Gorton said. "They're not looking at their impacts to the downstream."The pumping itself is not an illegal practice. Lucie has a permit allowing it to pump into the preserve, and Martin County leaders said there are not concrete regulation schedules governing the Savannas as a whole.That has raised a bigger question for local leaders: Who should be responsible for considering the consequences across the entire watershed?“I don't know that we can modify their permit, but I would hope that we'd be able to look at that and say, you know, do no harm, which is really what kind of — or shared adversity, I think, is a better way to say it,” Gorton said.One potential solution discussed by Martin County officials would put management of the Savannas watershed under one overarching organization rather than relying on decisions made by individual jurisdictions.“Once we get that water out, there's a larger discussion that we need to have, which is: What are we going to do to mitigate this in the future?” Gorton said.He suggested the water management district could potentially play a role."One such idea might be looking at treating the Savannas as a watershed that needs to be managed by one party," Gorton said. "Maybe it would be the water management district."Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi agreed that the current situation warrants another look."I agree with what your suggestion was, is that it just can't be whoever pumps fastest and first wins," Ciampi said.For people still dealing with the consequences in Jensen Beach, those discussions come as they search for answers, assistance and, in some cases, a dry place to call home.WPTV will continue following whether Martin County and other agencies develop a new plan for managing water in the Savannas and what changes could be made before another major rainfall event.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Following a brief pause, the Martin County Board of Commissioners announced on Tuesday that the county has reached a resolution to begin phased restoration of MARTY transit services. The county says it has reached a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit, LLC to begin the phased restoration of public transportation services following an abrupt disruption due to a contract breach by the prior vendor. Last month, MARTY public transit services in Martin County abruptly stopped after its operator withdrew from its contract due to rising operating costs. This left many people without a regular bus service. The county now says it will be taking a phased approach to resuming operations, prioritizing riders who rely on ADA paratransit services, then working towards restoring fixed-route services. See also: Delray Beach says new Florida law will block St. Patrick’s Day, Pride events For those who with disabilities who cannot use regular fixed-route bus services, ADA paratransit services are expected to resume on Thursday, Nov. Details regarding scheduling and reservations are available at 772-463-2822 , the county says. A start date for restoration of full services has yet to be announced. Our priority is to restore public transportation as quickly and responsibly as possible, with particular attention to residents who depend on these services to access essential needs, as well as fiscal responsibility to the taxpayer, said Ash Beecher, Martin County Transit Administrator. We recognize the disruption this has caused for our riders and the broader community, and we are working to reestablish service in a thoughtful, coordinated manner.

Martin County residents gathered at the commission chambers Tuesday morning to express their concerns about ongoing flooding in their neighborhoods and demand action from county leaders. "For 40 years, I’ve raised my family here, built my life here, and in the hours, watched everything we worked for become submerged in flood water and sewage," Jensen Beach resident Mary Berner said. Resident Lisa French described the impact of the flooding, saying, "Today, we’re homeless. We have nowhere to have Christmas. We don’t have much to come home to." Some residents questioned whether drainage infrastructure and development contributed to the flooding, while Yamila Rollan Escalona, who's with the Yaya por Vida Foundation, raised concerns about response efforts. MARTIN COUNTY FLOODING: Jensen Beach residents struggle with flooding and damaged homes after historic rainfall "Take Rich, a historic Black American in a Bahamian neighborhood inhabited and preserved for generations by a majority Black Americans. With a capital 'B.' They still have not been properly mitigated. Standing water, no pumps, no headlines, not a peep on social media, and just one article in the news today! Katrina much?" Rollan Escalona said. County leaders said crews are pumping water around the clock and assured residents that once the immediate flooding is addressed, they will explore ways to reduce future risks. Some proposed solutions include having one agency, such as the South Florida Water Management District, manage the nearby Savannas as a single watershed and exploring additional drainage options. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "I do expect you to make additional funding available to your staff today to mitigate this emergency as efficiently as possible. Thank you for your time and expect to continue to hear from us," resident Kyle Pond said. Commissioner Sarah Heard responded, saying, "Jensen Beach residents, we’ve heard you loud and clear. You are our top priority." County leaders also said they plan to review the county’s warning system and will address the flooding issue again at their next meeting, where they will provide updates and discuss a potential grant program. Martin County has signed a one-year emergency contract to restore the MARTY bus services, which will resume in phases. The service ended abruptly on Oct. 8 after the last vendor, Martin County Transit LLC, canceled services, citing rising costs of fuel and maintenance. The county signed the emergency contract with MTM Transit, which has operated these buses in the past. The first phase begins Thursday and will prioritize eligible riders with disabilities who cannot use the regular fixed-route bus service. For details on scheduling and reservations, residents should call 772-463-2822. As for regular services, there is still no official start date. The county is working to restore buses and rehire bus drivers who were let go by the previous vendor.

Lucie County animal shelter is making an urgent push to find homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month.The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency "Empty the Shelters" adoption event on Nov. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event.The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home in October.The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges.Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals.All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped.The event runs from 11 a.m. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Lucie.Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org.

Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

A Treasure Coast woman who lost her home two years ago to a tornado from Hurricane Milton has lost another home to devastating flooding in Fort Pierce."I'm starting to feel like I'm invincible at this point," says Terry Polk as she watched the debris pile of drywall and ruined furniture in front of her home get bigger.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The water in her home was measured in feet, not inches, as the heavy rain in the first weekend of November flooded her block."We were actually in the house," Polk said. "When we were wading around, like around knee-deep water, I started getting scared."She said they were rescued by kayaks and returned when the water receded, leaving so much damage. "You know, to keep your focus, you just have to realize there are people out there that have it way worse. There are people out there that are so much worse, you know, and I have to be thankful that we got out with our lives," she said. Two years ago she was living in the Spanish Lakes community of St. Lucie County when Hurricane Milton's winds created widespread tornadoes. One of the twisters, an EF3, struck the community, killing six people and destroying homes, including Terry's. "Terry is one of the most amazing people I've met," said friend Cindy McGee. "She's very strong, does a lot for the community, a lot for the neighborhood." Polk said she has flood insurance, but the damage is so extensive, she's not sure if there is enough coverage to fix everything.

Residents and farmers in western St. Lucie County are seeking answers and long-term drainage solutions after historic flooding left homes, farms and roads underwater last week.The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear concerns from people in the area, including farmers, residents and representatives from Save the Chimps. District members said the drainage system can handle only so much water during an extreme rainfall event and discussed engineering as part of a possible long-term plan.WATCH REPORT BELOW:Some of the hardest-hit areas are now seeing significant improvement, including Save the Chimps in western St. But residents and farmers say they want to know what can be done to reduce the risk of similar flooding during the next extreme rainfall event.For one resident, the flooding has already changed how they view their future in the area."I will be selling my house cause I am not going to risk my investment," the resident said during Monday's meeting.Water control district hears concerns from western St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear from people affected by the flooding.Farmers, residents and representatives of Save the Chimps attended as district members discussed the drainage system and the scale of last week's flooding.President Steve Cassens said there are limits to what the existing system can handle when extraordinary amounts of rain fall in a short period."If we have a rainfall event like that, my personal feeling is you can have gates open, shut, it doesn't matter," said Cassens. "We can manage water maybe 3, 4, 5, 6 inches. We can't manage water in the quantities that we got."District officials also discussed maintaining waterways and ditches, including concerns about a creek in Western Fort Pierce that serves as a primary drainage route. The district said it systematically cleans ditches within its boundaries.The district said it could examine engineering as part of developing a long-range plan.Conditions improve at Save the ChimpsSave the Chimps, a sanctuary in western St. Lucie County, was among the places hit hard by the flooding.WPTV previously reported that staff members had to use drones to deliver food to chimpanzees because several roads through the sanctuary were underwater.When WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache returned days later, staff said conditions had significantly improved."A short 40 hours after that, we're almost completely dry on our roads," said Mark Yohannan.The improvement came after days of challenges caused by standing water at the sanctuary.West Fort Pierce farmer raises concernsThe concerns extended beyond residential neighborhoods.Justin Akerley, who helps operate Saint Lucie Farm Preserve in west Fort Pierce, spoke later Monday at a Port St. Lucie City Council meeting after attending the water control district meeting.Akerley told council members he believes continued development is adding pressure to the area's drainage infrastructure."I just spent my morning in a meeting with the North St. Lucie River Water Control District trying to figure out what we can do to alleviate the water issues, and there's really no right answer except for stop building," Akerley said.Akerley shared a video with WPTV showing flooding at Saint Lucie Farm Preserve, a working agritourism farm operated by Akerley and Michael Hale. The farm produces hay, cut flowers, beef and assorted vegetables and hosts community agricultural events.Akerley told council members the consequences extend to other farms and families."I've got friends that have calves dying that are flooded; they can't get out," he said. "It's a terrible, terrible situation for everybody. There's people that have lost their homes."He urged city leaders to reconsider the effect future development could have on flooding and drainage."Just please reconsider because it's not a good situation for everybody, and it's only gonna get worse," Akerley said.Officials consider what comes nextDuring Monday's Port St. Lucie City Council meeting, Councilman David Pickett also called for greater scrutiny of flooding and the city's stormwater infrastructure.Pickett said he sent two memos to the city manager earlier in the week addressing floodwaters and wants the city to expedite a planned stormwater study rather than wait until 2029.He also raised concerns about flooding in Tradition and called for the city to examine stormwater systems before distributing certain stormwater fees to community development districts.Meanwhile, the North St. Lucie River Water Control District has said engineering options can be assessed as officials consider a long-term plan.For residents and farmers still recovering from last week's flooding, those discussions are now turning toward a larger question: what can be done before the next extreme rainfall event?This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Community members in Fort Pierce gathered Wednesday to honor veterans, military families, and those who continue to serve the country in a heartfelt ceremony. The event recognized the brave men and women who have worn the uniform and represented the United States Armed Forces. Dennis Mallon, who served in the U.S. Army from 1966 to 1968, shared his personal loss. "I lost my best friend," Mallon said. "He ended up going into the Marines, I ended up going in the Army, and he did the ultimate sacrifice. To this day, I miss him." The ceremony also expressed gratitude to military families for their support. I come from a military family," one attendee said. "Everything was pretty nice. I'm out here to support the veterans, and everything turned out pretty nice. I'm glad to be a part of it," Retired U.S. Army veteran Zachary Pressley said. Cynthia Shelton, representing the American Legion Post 171. Army veteran, who served from 1987 to 2021, highlighted the importance of supporting service members. "One of our members is deployed at this time, so we are also keeping her in our prayers because the wars are always going to be there, so we have to always show up and do our part," Shelton said. Vietnam veteran Dave Kauffman, who served in 1968, reflected on the progress made in honoring veterans. "When we came home from Vietnam, none of this existed. We were not welcomed home, and I think we learned from that, and we won't make that mistake again. It's heartwarming to see people coming out," Kauffman said. Members of Fort Pierce Central High School's JROTC attended the event, along with recent graduate Private First-Class Jason Salinas, now a U.S. "It's great that they're still doing things like this because it not only shows appreciation and love that we show due to the loss of veterans that we have, I'm so thankful that I'm here and able to follow in their footsteps so that I can still continue in their legacy and hold on to that no matter what," Salinas said. "I'm so thankful for the opportunity I was given and blessed with by not only my friends and family and the people that support me but also to God that gave me the opportunity to raise my right hand and take it further on," Salinas said. This year’s guest speaker, Sergeant Major Brian Huston, U.S. Army (Retired), shared a message of gratitude for veterans and those still serving, thanking them for answering the call.
