hero.headline: Fort Pierce veterans, military families honored at Veterans Day ceremony
hero.teaser: Veterans and Fort Pierce Central High School's JROTC joined the community Wednesday to recognize military service and the families who support it.
hero.body:
Veterans, military families and members of Fort Pierce Central High School's JROTC gathered in Fort Pierce on Wednesday for a Veterans Day ceremony honoring those who have served and those still in uniform. The event recognized service in the United States Armed Forces and the support military families provide.

Dennis Mallon, who served in the U.S. Army from 1966 to 1968, remembered his best friend, who joined the Marines and died while serving. "I lost my best friend," Mallon said. "He ended up going into the Marines, I ended up going in the Army, and he did the ultimate sacrifice. To this day, I miss him."

Vietnam veteran Dave Kauffman, who served in 1968, reflected on how the reception for veterans has changed. "When we came home from Vietnam, none of this existed. We were not welcomed home, and I think we learned from that, and we won't make that mistake again. It's heartwarming to see people coming out," Kauffman said.

Cynthia Shelton, an Army veteran who served from 1987 to 2021, represented American Legion Post 171 and emphasized continued support for service members. "One of our members is deployed at this time, so we are also keeping her in our prayers because the wars are always going to be there, so we have to always show up and do our part," Shelton said. Retired U.S. Army veteran Zachary Pressley also attended to support veterans and said he was glad to participate.

Recent graduate Private First-Class Jason Salinas attended alongside members of Fort Pierce Central High School's JROTC. Salinas expressed gratitude for the opportunity to follow veterans' footsteps and continue their legacy, as well as for the support of his friends and family. The ceremony's guest speaker, Sergeant Major Brian Huston, U.S. Army (Retired), thanked veterans and those still serving for answering the call.

hero.headline: Martin County signs emergency contract to restore MARTY bus service in phases
hero.body:
Martin County has signed a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit to restore MARTY bus service in phases, beginning Thursday with service prioritizing eligible riders with disabilities who cannot use regular fixed-route buses.

Regular fixed-route service remains suspended as the county works to restore buses and rehire drivers let go by the previous vendor. Residents can call 772-463-2822 for scheduling and reservation details for the first phase.

MARTY service ended abruptly on Oct. 8 after Martin County Transit LLC canceled services, citing rising fuel and maintenance costs. MTM Transit, the company hired under the emergency contract, has operated the buses in the past.
hero.article_text: Martin County has signed a one-year emergency contract to restore the MARTY bus services, which will resume in phases. The service ended abruptly on Oct. 8 after the last vendor, Martin County Transit LLC, canceled services, citing rising costs of fuel and maintenance. The county signed the emergency contract with MTM Transit, which has operated these buses in the past. The first phase begins Thursday and will prioritize eligible riders with disabilities who cannot use the regular fixed-route bus service. For details on scheduling and reservations, residents should call 772-463-2822. As for regular services, there is still no official start date. The county is working to restore buses and rehire bus drivers who were let go by the previous vendor.

cards.headline: Cleanup begins near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach as floodwaters recede
cards.teaser: Martin County pumping is helping residents begin cleanup after more than a week of flooding. A recovery assistance center is open at Hoke Library in Jensen Beach.
cards.body:
Residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are beginning to clean up their homes as Martin County pumping slowly lowers floodwaters that have stood for more than a week. The county began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to assess damage, while other residents are still waiting for the water to recede.

Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. Community volunteers are also collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families.

At Lisa French’s home, water that had reached more than a foot deep in some rooms has receded, leaving much of what she owns destroyed. Since early Wednesday morning, French, her husband and several neighbors have been removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard.

“You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said.

Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen, said volunteers have been collecting supplies for families affected by the flooding. She is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, and the event will serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance.

“The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County shelter to waive cat adoption fees after taking in 114 cats
hero.teaser: The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is planning an emergency, two-day adoption event after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home tied to an alleged animal hoarding case.
hero.body:
The Humane Society of St. Lucie County will waive adoption fees for all cats and kittens during an emergency, two-day adoption event after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case.

The shelter is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for the “Empty the Shelters” event to relieve overcrowding and make room to continue caring for animals. The case led to the arrest of Kimberly K. Robinson, 66, on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Police said those charges stemmed from veterinary findings for the first 29 cats evaluated.

All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event will take place at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road. Prospective adopters can view available pets at hsslc.org.
hero.article_text: Lucie County animal shelter is making an urgent push to find homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency "Empty the Shelters" adoption event on Nov. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

cards.headline: Flood damages Fort Pierce woman’s childhood home; insurance falls short
cards.teaser: Terri Polk is determined to rebuild after flooding severely damaged her childhood home. She previously lost her Spanish Lakes home to a tornado during Hurricane Milton.
cards.body:
Floodwaters severely damaged Fort Pierce resident Terri Polk’s childhood home, leaving her facing a second major loss in two years and repair costs her flood insurance will not fully cover. She is determined to rebuild after previously losing her home in the Spanish Lakes community to a tornado during Hurricane Milton.

Polk had moved back into her childhood home to care for her mother, who has Alzheimer’s. Her parents built the house, which has long been a gathering place for the family. “My mother’s door has always been open to everyone in the family,” she said. “This breaks your heart because I grew up in this house, I actually grew up here.”

Floodwaters rushed into the house last Monday. “In the morning, the water was up to the tops of the beds,” Polk said. After the water receded, her belongings, including her bed and bookcases, ended up in a pile on the front lawn. The house is now filled with dehumidifiers as she works through the damage.

Polk said she hasn’t slept in days as she tries to process the loss. With flood insurance covering only part of the damage, she remains committed to rebuilding. “No is not the answer; quit is not an option,” she said. “I’m not going to give up.”

hero.headline: Jensen Beach residents begin cleanup as floodwater recedes near Hyline Drive
hero.body:
Some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are beginning damage assessments and cleanup as Martin County pumping slowly lowers floodwater that has stood for more than a week. The county began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to start assessing damage while other homes remain flooded.

County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. Community volunteers are also collecting supplies and organizing a fundraiser for affected families.

For Lisa French, the receding water has allowed cleanup to begin after flooding reached more than a foot deep in some rooms of her home. Much of what she owns has been destroyed. Since early Wednesday morning, French, her husband and several neighbors have been removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard.

“You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said.

Other residents are still waiting for the water to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said the flooding was unlike anything she had experienced there. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said.

Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen, said volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. She is organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, and the event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance.

“The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said.

hero.headline: Stuart parade, local ceremonies were planned for Veterans Day on the Treasure Coast
hero.body:
Stuart’s Veterans Day parade was set to start at 10 a.m. Wednesday, Nov. 11, on East Ocean Boulevard and finish at Memorial Park. The parade and ceremony were part of a day of events honoring military veterans across the Treasure Coast. Plans in Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties included ceremonies, music, a lunch and a gathering for veterans. Other communities in Palm Beach and Okeechobee counties also scheduled observances, with events running from early morning into the evening.

In Port St. Lucie, a free Veterans Day ceremony was planned for 11 a.m. at Veterans Memorial Park, 2100 S.E. Veterans Memorial Parkway. The program included remarks, music, a rifle salute, a flyover and Taps. With seating limited, attendees were encouraged to come early and bring a chair. Fort Pierce also scheduled its Veterans Day ceremony for 11 a.m. at Veterans Memorial Park. After that observance, a free lunch and live entertainment were planned for noon at VFW Post 8058, 3475 Douglas Ave.

Indian River County’s calendar listed a Veterans Day Observance at 5:30 p.m. Wednesday. It also included Veterans Meet Up, a gathering for veterans scheduled for 6 to 8 p.m. at Our House Network in Vero Beach. In Okeechobee County, the Okeechobee KOA RV Resort planned a Veterans Day celebration from 5 to 8 p.m. Central Elementary scheduled its celebration for 8:30 a.m., and the school invited families to share photographs of veterans. Those events added a school celebration and an evening resort gathering to the region’s plans for the holiday.

Palm Beach County’s schedule began with Wellington’s parade at 8:15 a.m. from Village Hall, 12300 Forest Hill Blvd., followed by an 8:30 a.m. ceremony at the Wellington Veterans Memorial at Forest Hill and South Shore boulevards. Delray Beach planned a 9 a.m. ceremony at the Vintage Gym at Old School Square. North Palm Beach’s ceremony was set for 9 a.m. at Veterans Memorial Park, 303 Anchorage Drive. Royal Palm Beach scheduled its ceremony from 9 a.m. to noon at the Cultural Center, 151 Civic Center Way. Palm Beach Gardens planned an 11 a.m. salute at Veterans Plaza Amphitheater, featuring a keynote speaker and the high school chorus. hero.headline: Martin County votes 3-2 to pursue quiet zones at three railroad crossings
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted 3-2 Tuesday to pursue train quiet zones at three railroad crossings in Jensen Beach and near Mariner Sands, reversing last year’s unanimous rejection of quiet zones. The decision followed complaints about train horns and narrowed an initial proposal covering all 27 crossings in the county.

The first crossings to be worked on are at County Line Road and Skyline Drive in Jensen Beach, along with a third crossing on Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound near Mariner Sands. Commissioners first considered a motion to turn all 27 crossings into quiet zones. A second motion narrowed the scope and passed.

Opponents raised safety concerns, while supporters described train noise as a quality-of-life issue. “The horn all day and all night. And as I’m listening to that noisy disruption, I can visualize the intersection with four gates down, deployed, and cars safely behind them with that horn pointlessly bothering people,” said Doug Farley, a quiet zone supporter.

The city of Stuart recently received a $1.86 million grant to enhance rail corridor safety. In Palm Beach County, Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens recently established quiet zones.

hero.headline: Family seeks North Boulevard safety changes after St. Lucie County teen killed
hero.body:
The family of 18-year-old Omari Linzell Williams is calling for sidewalks, speed bumps and lighting on North Boulevard after he was struck and killed while walking to get groceries in St. Lucie County. His mother, Witney Williams, and aunt, Sharon Garcia, are seeking answers about the crash and plan to launch a petition in his name to make the roadway safer.

Investigators said Williams was walking along the westbound lane of North Boulevard around 6 p.m. Tuesday when a 30-year-old driver struck him. According to investigators, the driver was unable to see Williams before the collision. The driver was uninjured and cooperated with investigators. The traffic homicide investigation remains ongoing.

Garcia said floodwaters on the opposite side of the road prevented her nephew from walking there. That description of roadside conditions came from the family. Relatives said Williams had left home to pick up groceries. “At this moment they don't have a car and he was walking to the store to get the items and he didn't make it very far,” Garcia said.

Witney Williams said she became concerned after seeing a social media post and being unable to reach her son by phone. She ran from the house and rushed toward the scene, hoping to reach him before he died. “We miss him and we just want answers,” Garcia said. “We just want to know like any family, what happened.”

His mother described Williams as a caring older brother to his six siblings who regularly offered to help her. Relatives said he also used an online platform to support people struggling through difficult periods. After his death, people contacted the family to share how he had helped them.

Witney Williams said she wants safety improvements to protect other children. “We need sidewalks, we need speed bumps and we need lights,” she said. Garcia said the planned petition would seek changes to make North Boulevard safer.

The family plans to hold a candlelight vigil at 6 p.m. Friday at Lakewood Park in the Fort Pierce area. Relatives, friends and community members will gather to remember Williams. The family also started a fundraiser to help with funeral expenses.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium
cards.teaser: The city plans to reimburse developers up to $27.5 million through tax increment financing. The stadium at “Walton and One” will become the home of Port St. Lucie Sports Club in 2028.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved the site plan for a 6,000-seat soccer stadium at the “Walton and One” development area. The city plans to reimburse the developers up to $27.5 million through tax increment financing.

The stadium is expected to cost between $50 million and $80 million. When the reimbursement plan was announced, the city said taxpayer funds would not be used directly.

The stadium will become the home of Port St. Lucie Sports Club starting in 2028. The team is slated to begin play in the United Soccer League in March 2027.

Representatives for Port St. Lucie SC said in July that groundbreaking for the stadium was anticipated this year. Plans target November for the start of construction.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County shelter to waive adoption fees after taking in 114 cats
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of St. Lucie County faces a capacity crunch after taking in cats from a Port St. Lucie home linked to an alleged hoarding case.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of St. Lucie County will waive adoption fees for all cats and kittens during a two-day emergency adoption event after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home last month. The shelter says the intake has created a capacity crunch.

The shelter is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for the “Empty the Shelters” event, hoping to free up space to continue caring for the animals. The cats came from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman’s arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges.

All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event will take place at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Lucie. Available pets can be viewed at hsslc.org.
cards.article_text: Lucie County animal shelter is making an urgent push to find homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency "Empty the Shelters" adoption event on Nov. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

hero.headline: Martin County weighs unified Savannas management after Jensen Beach flooding
hero.body:
Martin County officials are considering putting the Savannas watershed under one organization after flooding damaged or destroyed homes in Jensen Beach. The proposal comes amid concerns about the downstream effects of Port St. Lucie's permitted pumping of floodwater into the Savannas Preserve following historic rainfall on the Treasure Coast.

At a Martin County Commission meeting, Public Works Director James Gorton suggested that the water management district could oversee the watershed rather than leaving management decisions to individual jurisdictions. “One such idea might be looking at treating the Savannas as a watershed that needs to be managed by one party,” Gorton said. “Maybe it would be the water management district.”

Officials said Port St. Lucie pumped floodwater into the preserve before water flowed south toward Jensen Beach neighborhoods. Gorton said the city pumped Monday and Tuesday morning, stopping Tuesday morning. Port St. Lucie has a permit allowing it to pump into the preserve. Residents believe pumping from areas to the north contributed to water moving south and overflowing into their neighborhoods.

Gorton raised concerns about jurisdictions focusing on water levels within their own watersheds rather than downstream consequences. “They're just looking at the water levels that are in their watershed,” he said. “They're not looking at their impacts to the downstream.” He also acknowledged the challenge posed by the storm: “The severity of that rainfall caught us unprepared,” Gorton said.

The flooding and damage came days after the historic rainfall stopped. Tiffany Kincaid, whose home was devastated, said her family believed protections were in place until rising water forced them to leave. “I've never seen anything like this, not this level of devastation that has been sort of sitting in water for now eight days,” Kincaid said.

Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi supported reconsidering how the watershed is managed. “I agree with what your suggestion was, is that it just can't be whoever pumps fastest and first wins,” Ciampi said.

Gorton framed unified management as a potential way to reduce future flooding. “Once we get that water out, there's a larger discussion that we need to have, which is: What are we going to do to mitigate this in the future?” he said.

cards.headline: Cleanup begins near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach as floodwaters slowly recede
cards.teaser: Martin County pumping has allowed some residents to begin removing damaged belongings while others remain flooded. A recovery assistance center is open at the Hoke Library, and volunteers are collecting supplies.
cards.body:
Some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach have begun cleaning their homes after more than a week of standing floodwater, while others are still waiting for the water to recede. Martin County began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to start assessing the damage.

Lisa French, her husband and several neighbors began removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard early Wednesday morning. Water had reached more than a foot deep in some rooms of her home. It has since receded, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said.

Other residents continue to wait for floodwaters to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said the flooding is unlike anything she has experienced there. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said.

Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. Community volunteers are also collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families, according to Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen.

Macpherson is organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, and the event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said.

hero.headline: Family seeks North Boulevard safety improvements after 18-year-old killed
hero.body:
The family of 18-year-old Omari Linzell Williams is calling for sidewalks, speed bumps and lighting on North Boulevard in St. Lucie County after a driver struck and killed him while he was walking to buy groceries. The traffic homicide investigation remains ongoing.

His mother, Witney Williams, said she wants changes to protect other children. “We need sidewalks, we need speed bumps and we need lights,” she said. His aunt, Sharon Garcia, said the family plans to launch a petition in his name to make the roadway safer. The family is also seeking answers about the circumstances of the crash.

Investigators said Williams was walking along the westbound lane of North Boulevard around 6 p.m. Tuesday when a 30-year-old driver struck him. According to investigators, the driver was unable to see Williams before the collision. The driver cooperated with investigators.

Relatives said Williams had left home to pick up groceries because the family did not have a vehicle. Garcia said floodwaters affected where he could walk. “There was floodwaters on the opposite side of the road so he couldn't walk on that side,” she said.

Witney Williams said she became concerned after seeing a social media post and being unable to reach her son by phone. She rushed toward the scene. “I was just praying that I'd get there before he took his last breath and I didn't make it,” she said.

His mother described him as a caring older brother to his six siblings who regularly helped her. After his death, relatives said people reached out to describe how he had supported them through difficult periods. The family learned he had used an online platform to connect with people who were struggling.

“It sucks that I lost mine, but I'm going to fight to make sure this doesn't happen to another kid,” his mother said.

The family plans to hold a candlelight vigil at 6 p.m. Friday at Lakewood Park in the Fort Pierce area. Relatives, friends and community members will have an opportunity to remember Williams. The family also started a fundraiser to help with funeral expenses.

hero.headline: Flooding leaves Vero Beach family farm’s citrus groves underwater for over a week
hero.body:
Flooding has left citrus groves at Greene Sugars Farm in Vero Beach underwater for more than a week despite heavy pumping every morning and night, putting the multigenerational family farm’s crops, trees and livestock in jeopardy.

Aubrey Greene said the farm received more than 10 inches of rain in a single night during last week’s flooding across South Florida. Water has flooded the citrus groves from trunk to trunk, and the farm has continued pumping twice daily.

Greene Sugars Farm has 800 acres of lemon trees, 50 acres of sugar belle trees and thousands of cattle. The farm produces roughly 60,000 to 80,000 boxes of citrus a year and has a contract with Coca-Cola.

Greene said the farm had a great citrus season last year and had anticipated another good year before the flooding threatened its crops, trees and livestock.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton and One
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved the site plan for a 6,000-seat soccer stadium at the "Walton and One" development area. The city plans to reimburse the developers up to $27.5 million through tax increment financing.

The stadium is expected to cost between $50 million and $80 million. When the reimbursement plan was announced, the city said taxpayer funds would not be used directly.

The stadium is expected to become the home of the "Port St. Lucie Sports Club" in 2028. The team is slated to begin play in the United Soccer League in March 2027, ahead of its planned move into the stadium.

Representatives for Port St. Lucie SC said in July that groundbreaking for the stadium was anticipated this year. Current plans target November for the start of construction.

hero.headline: Cleanup begins near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach as floodwaters recede
hero.body:
Some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are beginning to clean up their homes after more than a week of standing floodwater. Martin County began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to assess the damage as water slowly recedes. Other residents are still waiting for floodwaters to recede.

Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. Community volunteers are also collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families.

At Lisa French’s home, French, her husband and several neighbors began removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard early Wednesday morning. Water had reached more than a foot deep in some rooms several days earlier. It has since receded from the home, but much of what French owns has been destroyed. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said.

Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, is among the residents still waiting for the water to recede. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said.

Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen, said volunteers have been gathering supplies. She is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food. The event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Veterans Day ceremony honors veterans across generations
cards.teaser: Vietnam veterans, a 98-year-old World War II veteran and Port St. Lucie High School Junior ROTC participants joined Wednesday's ceremony at Veterans Memorial Park.
cards.body:
Veterans from across generations gathered Wednesday at Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie for the annual Veterans Day ceremony, including Vietnam veterans and a 98-year-old World War II veteran. Residents of all ages filled the park, and the Port St. Lucie High School Junior ROTC attended in force.

Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service. “It's all like my whole history. I started in transportation. I think it's very important. I enlisted and was not supposed to go but ended up over there,” Greene said. Fellow Vietnam War veteran Wayne Thomas said the day properly honors their service.

Among those attending was 98-year-old World War II veteran Robert Vogel, who encouraged people to take part in events supporting veterans. “I'm one of the few left. I would really encourage anyone to come to these events because they're really important to support the veterans,” Vogel said.

Retired Air Force Master Sgt. Vincent Lavelle Jr. delivered the keynote address. The Port St. Lucie community band played songs from each branch of service, prompting service members in the crowd to stand when their branch's song played. The ceremony also featured a flyover by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office helicopter.

hero.headline: Martin County flooding affects 77 homes; recovery help available at Hoke Library
hero.body:
Flooding affected 77 homes in Martin County, with about 24 estimated destroyed, according to Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite. Residents can get recovery assistance at Hoke Library in Jensen Beach while awaiting word on federal aid. Some homes took on three to five feet of water, Waite said.

The Multi-Agency Resource Center at Hoke Library, 1150 NW Jack Williams Way, connects residents with state agencies and local nonprofits. The recovery center is open Wednesday despite regular library services being closed for Veterans Day. The county lists the center’s operating days as Wednesday through Saturday until further notice, with the center closed Sundays. More agencies and services will be added throughout the week, according to the county.

Martin County is also accepting applications for state disaster housing assistance. Households must meet income requirements, and residents can call 772-320-3169 for details. Residents can report flood damage and complete a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Florida announced Monday that it had requested a presidential major disaster declaration for the flooding. If FEMA Individual Assistance is authorized for Martin County, eligible households could apply for help with temporary housing and essential home repairs.

At Tuesday’s commission meeting, Jensen Beach residents said flooding had forced them from their homes and pressed county leaders about drainage and how they were warned. Waite told commissioners that assessment teams planned to visit each of the 77 affected homes to document damage. A week earlier, streets throughout Jensen Beach’s Skyline Heights neighborhood were underwater, and residents used kayaks to check on homes and neighbors.

Part of Hyline Drive remained underwater Wednesday as cleanup began at Lisa French’s home in Skyline Heights. Workers carried out belongings touched by floodwater, leaving cabinets, furniture and drywall in the front yard. French said hers was the first home in the neighborhood being cleared out and gutted. She and her family are staying with her parents while waiting to hear about longer-term housing. She said they do not have flood insurance.

Alaura Macpherson, co-founder of Quit Messing With Jensen, collected cleanup supplies for affected families at the Hoke Library resource center Wednesday. She also helped French’s family clear out flood damage at their home.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County formalizes flooding emergency as residents seek drainage investigations
hero.body:
St. Lucie County formalized its emergency declaration after days of heavy rain and flooding as Creekside and White City residents asked commissioners to investigate drainage problems and prevent future flooding. At the same meeting, commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change that could allow nearly 500 homes on roughly 34 acres near South 25th Street and West Midway Road.

The emergency declaration covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems. Residents asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems and explain how to prevent future flooding.

Creekside residents called for an engineering review of their neighborhood and the surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also requested a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012.

Drainage was also a concern in the discussion of the proposed land-use change near South 25th Street and West Midway Road. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed.

The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. Commissioners questioned how the site handles drainage as residents sought answers about the recent flooding.

A residential designation could allow up to 15 homes per acre on the property, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request.

hero.headline: MARTY begins phased return in Martin County after monthlong shutdown
hero.body:
MARTY public transportation is returning in stages in Martin County after regular bus service was suspended for more than a month. The county expects ADA paratransit to resume first, with the U.S. Highway 1 and Indiantown routes following. More service will be introduced as buses are made ready and drivers become available, according to the county. The gradual restart follows the Oct. 8 shutdown, when the county’s transit provider abruptly stopped operating. That interruption left people who depended on MARTY looking for other ways to reach their jobs, shop for groceries and attend medical appointments.

For some passengers, the loss of bus service was especially difficult because injuries or disabilities limited their transportation options. A rider identified as Joe said he had received no advance notice that service would stop. “No warning at all. Zero,” he said. He described injuries that made it difficult for him to get around without the bus. “I've had two broken necks, three broken backs. I can't feel my feet, so I'm not getting anywhere,” he said. His experience reflected the difficulty the shutdown created for riders whose mobility limitations made alternatives hard to find.

United Way of Martin County began helping residents arrange essential trips through its Ride United program during the disruption. Carol Houwaart-Diez with United Way said the organization offered the county help after MARTY stopped running. “We made the call to the county administrator and said, 'Hey, how can we help?'” she said. “And we have a ride program that helps provide critical services in our community, and they said, 'Please help us.'” The nonprofit used Lyft to arrange transportation, providing 754 rides for 108 individual clients during the shutdown. Those trips took people to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and physical therapy.

The temporary rides did not meet every passenger’s needs. Houwaart-Diez said the Lyft vehicles used by the program generally could not accommodate people who were fully wheelchair-bound. “For those that were fully wheelchair bound, we couldn't help them, which made me sad,” she said. “We did look into to see if we could do that.” Restoring ADA paratransit is therefore an important part of the restart for riders with disabilities who could not use the Lyft option. United Way intends to keep offering other transportation help while MARTY rebuilds service. “Once that starts, we still will be able to provide the other services until everything gets back up in full gear,” Houwaart-Diez said.

cards.headline: Crews deploy two additional pumps for flooded Hyline area in Jensen Beach
cards.teaser: Martin County crews were setting up hoses on Jensen Beach Boulevard on Monday. Draining the flooded Hyline area could take at least a week, Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.
cards.body:
Martin County crews deployed two additional pumps to help drain the flooded Hyline area in Jensen Beach, Public Works Director Jim Gorton said. The pumping process could take at least a week or longer.

Crews were setting up hoses on Jensen Beach Boulevard on Monday to begin pumping water out of the Hyline Pond. Residents remained trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall.

Gorton said crews were pumping out a receiving pond as part of the effort. Water from the Hyline area must first move to that pond before it can be drained away.

“We've deployed two additional pumps up to that area. And what we're doing is pumping out the receiving pond, because we have to move the water from the Hyline area to another pond and then drain it out of that pond,” Gorton said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County rejects land-use change that could allow nearly 500 homes
hero.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change that could allow nearly 500 homes on roughly 34 acres near South 25th Street and West Midway Road. The decision came as commissioners questioned drainage at the low-lying property and residents sought action after recent flooding. County staff had recommended approving the change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers.

An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The site sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto neighboring properties. A residential designation could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion.

At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems and explain how to prevent future flooding. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of their neighborhood and the surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also requested a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. “I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us,” one resident said.

White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. The declaration covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

hero.headline: Flooding affects 77 Martin County homes; recovery help available at Hoke Library
hero.body:
Flooding affected 77 homes in Martin County, and residents can get recovery help Wednesday at Hoke Library in Jensen Beach. The county is also accepting applications for state disaster housing assistance for households that meet income requirements.

Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite gave commissioners the count at Tuesday’s commission meeting. She said assessment teams planned to visit each home to document the damage. Jensen Beach residents told commissioners that flooding had forced them from their homes and pressed county leaders about drainage and how they were warned.

The Multi-Agency Resource Center is at Hoke Library, 1150 NW Jack Williams Way. It is open Wednesday despite the closure of regular library services for Veterans Day. State agencies and local nonprofits are connecting residents with recovery resources, and the county says more agencies and services will be added throughout the week. The center operates Wednesday through Saturday until further notice and is closed Sundays.

Residents can call 772-320-3169 for details about state disaster housing assistance and its income requirements. They can also report flood damage and complete a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page.

Florida announced Monday that it had requested a presidential major disaster declaration for the flooding. FEMA Individual Assistance, if authorized for Martin County, could help eligible households pay for expenses such as temporary housing and essential home repairs.

cards.headline: Martin County ADA paratransit expected to resume Thursday under emergency contract
cards.teaser: Eligible MARTY paratransit riders can call 772-463-2822 for scheduling and reservation information. Martin County will announce fixed-route start dates as each restoration phase is finalized.
cards.body:
Martin County expects to resume MARTY ADA paratransit service Thursday under a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit, LLC, beginning a phased restoration of public transportation. Paratransit serves eligible riders with disabilities who are unable to use regular fixed-route buses.

MARTY customer service representatives are contacting active registered paratransit riders directly about the return of service. Riders can call 772-463-2822 for information about scheduling and reservations.

The county announced the phased approach Tuesday after its previous contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement last month, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees. County officials described the interruption as an abrupt disruption caused by a contract breach involving the previous vendor.

Fixed-route service will return as buses are prepared and drivers become available. The Indiantown route will be among the priorities. The county will announce start dates, schedules and rider instructions as each phase is finalized.

“Our priority is to restore public transportation as quickly and responsibly as possible, with particular attention to residents who depend on these services to access essential needs, as well as fiscal responsibility to the taxpayer,” Martin County Transit Administrator Ash Beecher said.

Beecher acknowledged that the disruption has affected riders and the broader community and said the county is working to reestablish service in a coordinated manner. During the interruption, United Way of Martin County helped coordinate transportation for people with critical travel needs.

Residents can find service updates through Martin County's transit website or call transit customer service at 772-463-2860.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach family seeks housing and repair funding after flooding destroys home interior
cards.teaser: Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission after flooding displaced them and their two young boys. They are seeking longer-term housing and money to repair their Jensen Beach home.
cards.body:
A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for longer-term housing and money to repair their home after pleading for help before the Martin County Commission. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, said floodwater destroyed much of their home's interior and left them trying to find a more permanent place to live while they work toward returning home.

“Today we are homeless,” Lisa French told commissioners. “We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to.” The family said the house was unsafe to enter. Lisa French described the losses: “Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture.” She said the home's floorboards were outside.

Historic rainfall across South Florida and the Treasure Coast surrounded the family's neighborhood with floodwater, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors. Much of the water receded days later, leaving extensive damage. Lisa French sought assistance at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people affected by the flooding. The family is trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing housing.

French said her home flooded days after the rain stopped. Martin County said the home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas. French questioned whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to the flooding at her home. “They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas,” she said.

French said she worries the family could face a significant financial gap even if additional assistance becomes available. “Who's going to fill in the gaps?” she said. She wants her boys to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain. Despite the damage, the family remains hopeful about returning. “We just want to go home,” she said.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach family appeals to Martin County commissioners for help after flooding
cards.teaser: Lisa and Jeremy French are seeking more permanent housing and money to repair their flood-damaged home, which they say remains unsafe to enter.
cards.body:
A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding appealed to the Martin County Commission for help finding more permanent housing and paying to rebuild their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, say the house remains unsafe to enter even as floodwaters have receded.

Through tears, the couple described their family's situation to commissioners. “Today we are homeless,” Lisa French told commissioners. “We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to.”

Historic rainfall across South Florida and the Treasure Coast left floodwater surrounding the family's neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors. Days later, much of the water has receded, but extensive damage remains inside the French home. Lisa French said the flooding destroyed much of what the family had accumulated over the years.

“My floorboards are outside,” she said. “Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture.”

Lisa French sought assistance at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people affected by the flooding. The family is trying to secure a more permanent place to live while determining how to pay for repairs.

French said her home flooded days after the rain stopped. Martin County said the home is near the Savannah Preserves, where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas. French questioned whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to the flooding at her home, claiming water was dumped there Monday and Tuesday.

French said she worries the family could face a significant financial gap even if additional aid becomes available. “Who's going to fill in the gaps?” she said.

She wants her boys to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain. Despite the damage, the family remains hopeful about returning. “We just want to go home,” French said.

Questions also arose at the meeting about the school district’s decision to keep schools open during Monday’s flooding. The district is expected to address those concerns at its meeting next Tuesday.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat stadium at Walton and One
cards.teaser: The city plans to reimburse developers up to $27.5 million through tax increment financing. The stadium is expected to cost between $50 million and $80 million.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council approved the site plan for a 6,000-seat soccer stadium at the Walton and One development area. The city plans to reimburse the developers up to $27.5 million through tax increment financing.

The stadium is expected to cost between $50 million and $80 million. When the plan was announced, the city said taxpayer funds would not be used directly. The stadium will be home to the Port St. Lucie Sports Club starting in 2028, while the team is slated to begin play in the United Soccer League in March 2027.

Representatives for Port St. Lucie SC said in July that groundbreaking for the stadium was anticipated this year, with plans targeting November.

The first crossings targeted for quiet-zone work are at County Line Road and Skyline Drive in Jensen Beach and along Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound near Mariner Sands. Commissioners approved the narrower scope through a second motion.

Opponents raised safety concerns, while supporters described train noise as a quality-of-life issue. Quiet-zone supporter Doug Farley questioned the need for horns at crossings with gates deployed. “The horn all day and all night. And as I'm listening to that noisy disruption, I can visualize the intersection with four gates down, deployed, and cars safely behind them with that horn pointlessly bothering people,” Farley said.

The Martin County vote authorizes work toward quiet zones, while St. Lucie County has already established a quiet zone at three crossings in its southern end. Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens in Palm Beach County also recently established quiet zones. The city of Stuart recently received a $1.86 million grant to enhance rail corridor safety.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach family asks Martin County commissioners for flood recovery help
cards.teaser: Lisa and Jeremy French are seeking more permanent housing and money to rebuild their flood-damaged Jensen Beach home, where they want to return with their two young boys.
cards.body:
A Jensen Beach family displaced by flooding appealed to the Martin County Commission for help securing more permanent housing and rebuilding their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, are trying to pay for repairs after floodwater destroyed much of the home's interior.

“Today we are homeless,” Lisa French told commissioners. “We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to.” The couple described their situation through tears and said their goal is to return to the home where they want their sons to continue growing up.

Historic rainfall across South Florida and the Treasure Coast left the family's neighborhood surrounded by floodwater, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors. Much of the water receded days later, but the family said the home was unsafe to enter. “My floorboards are outside,” Lisa French said. She said the flooding destroyed the family's appliances, cabinets and every piece of furniture.

Lisa French sought assistance at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people affected by the flooding. The family is looking for a more permanent place to stay while determining how to cover the cost of rebuilding. She said she worries that even additional aid could leave a significant financial gap. “Who's going to fill in the gaps?” she said.

French said the home flooded days after the rain stopped. Martin County said the property is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas. French questioned whether actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to the flooding at her home. That concern is her account, distinct from the county's explanation of natural water flow.

Despite the damage and uncertainty over repair costs, the family hopes to return. “We just want to go home,” Lisa French said. “Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family.”

cards.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved the site plan for a 6,000-seat soccer stadium at the "Walton and One" development area. The stadium is expected to cost between $50 million and $80 million.

Representatives for Port St. Lucie SC said in July that groundbreaking was anticipated this year, with current plans targeting November.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County residents demand drainage improvements after historic flooding
hero.body:
At Tuesday night’s Board of County Commissioners meeting, St. Lucie County residents demanded improvements to retention and drainage systems, along with answers about the county’s response to last week’s historic flooding. Dozens spoke during public comment, criticizing the response and calling for improvements to prevent future disasters.

“I lost everything; I’m a 73-year-old widow,” one resident said. Another woman said she had been living in a motel since last Monday and had returned home from vacation because of the flooding. “We don’t need another explanation on how historic this rainfall was. We need to make sure this never happens again,” another resident said.

Questions also arose at the meeting about the school district’s decision to keep schools open during Monday’s flooding. The district is expected to address those concerns at its meeting next Tuesday.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach family asks Martin County commissioners for housing and flood repair help
cards.teaser: Lisa and Jeremy French are seeking longer-term housing and money to repair their flood-damaged Jensen Beach home, where they hope to return with their two young boys.
cards.body:
Lisa and Jeremy French appealed to the Martin County Commission for help securing longer-term housing and paying for repairs after flooding displaced their family from their Jensen Beach home. The couple, who have two young boys, said the house is unsafe to enter and that they want to return home.

“Today we are homeless,” Lisa French told commissioners as the couple described their situation through tears. She said the family needs a more permanent place to live while determining how to pay for the extensive damage inside the house.

Historic rainfall left floodwater surrounding the family’s neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors. Much of the water receded days later, but the damage remained. Lisa French said the flooding destroyed appliances, cabinets and every piece of furniture. “My floorboards are outside,” she said.

The family has sought assistance at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people affected by the flooding. Lisa French said the home flooded days after the rain stopped. Martin County said the house is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas. She questioned whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to the flooding at her home.

Lisa French said she worries the family could face a significant financial gap even if additional aid becomes available. “Who's going to fill in the gaps?” she said. She wants her boys to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach house the family worked hard to maintain.

Despite the damage, the family remains hopeful about returning. “We just want to go home,” Lisa French said. “Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family.”

hero.headline: Veterans Day events today include Stuart parade, Fort Pierce ceremony
hero.body:
A parade in Stuart, a ceremony in Fort Pierce and evening events in Indian River County are among the Veterans Day observances scheduled for today, Wednesday, Nov. 11. Communities across the Treasure Coast will honor military veterans with parades, music and gatherings. Stuart’s Veterans Day Parade and Ceremony starts at 10 a.m. on East Ocean Boulevard and ends at Memorial Park. In St. Lucie County, a free ceremony begins at 11 a.m. at Veterans Memorial Park, 2100 S.E. Veterans Memorial Parkway. That program features remarks, musical selections, a rifle salute, a flyover and Taps. With limited seating available, organizers encourage attendees to come early and bring a chair.

Fort Pierce’s Veterans Day ceremony also starts at 11 a.m. at Veterans Memorial Park. Afterward, VFW Post 8058 will host a free lunch and live entertainment beginning at noon at 3475 Douglas Ave. Indian River County’s calendar includes two evening events: a Veterans Day Observance at 5:30 p.m. and a Veterans Meet Up from 6 to 8 p.m. The meet-up is a gathering for veterans at Our House Network in Vero Beach. In Okeechobee County, Central Elementary has a Veterans Day celebration scheduled for 8:30 a.m., and the school invited families to share photographs of veterans.

Palm Beach County’s morning events begin with Wellington’s parade at 8:15 a.m., departing from Village Hall, 12300 Forest Hill Blvd. A ceremony follows at 8:30 a.m. at the Wellington Veterans Memorial at Forest Hill and South Shore boulevards. Delray Beach has a 9 a.m. ceremony at the Vintage Gym at Old School Square. North Palm Beach’s ceremony also begins at 9 a.m., at Veterans Memorial Park, 303 Anchorage Drive. Royal Palm Beach’s observance runs from 9 a.m. to noon at the Royal Palm Beach Cultural Center, 151 Civic Center Way.

Later programs include Palm Beach Gardens’ Veterans Salute Celebration at 11 a.m. at the Veterans Plaza Amphitheater, with a keynote speaker and a performance by the Palm Beach Gardens High School Chorus. Boca Raton’s free Red, White & Boca event runs from 4 to 7 p.m. at Mizner Park Amphitheater, 590 Plaza Real. Its lineup includes live music, speakers, a marketplace featuring veterans and a classic car show. Lake Worth Beach has a Veterans Day celebration scheduled for 5 p.m. In Okeechobee County, the Okeechobee KOA RV Resort will hold its Veterans Day celebration from 5 to 8 p.m.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie City Council approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved the site plan for a 6,000-seat soccer stadium at the "Walton and One" development area. The stadium is planned to become the home of the Port St. Lucie Sports Club in 2028.

The stadium is expected to cost between $50 million and $80 million. The city plans to reimburse developers up to $27.5 million through tax increment financing. When the plan was announced, the city said taxpayer funds would not be used directly.

The club is slated to begin play in the United Soccer League in March 2027, ahead of the stadium’s planned opening. Representatives for Port St. Lucie SC said in July that groundbreaking was anticipated this year, with plans targeting November.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County district announces Nov. 9 school reopening after flooding
cards.teaser: The district said most bus stops would operate as usual, with temporary changes possible because of road conditions. Recovery resources include information about government assistance.
cards.body:
The school district in St. Lucie County announced plans to reopen all schools Monday, Nov. 9, after flooding it described as historic. The district said most bus stops would operate as usual, though road conditions could require some stops to be temporarily relocated.

Under the district’s transportation notification plan, families with affected stops were to receive a call from the SLPS Transportation Department on Sunday. The district told families their child’s regular stop would remain unchanged unless they received a call.

The superintendent thanked families for their patience and praised bus drivers and school staff who worked beyond their usual hours to help students get home safely.

The district also posted recovery resources for families affected by the flooding, including information about government assistance.

hero.headline: Martin County reaches one-year emergency contract for phased MARTY transit return
hero.body:
Martin County has reached a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit, LLC to restore MARTY public transportation services in phases, starting with riders who depend on ADA paratransit. The Martin County Board of Commissioners announced the agreement Tuesday after an abrupt service disruption last month.

The county expects ADA paratransit services to resume Thursday for people with disabilities who cannot use regular fixed-route buses. Restoring fixed-route service will follow the initial focus on paratransit riders. Riders can call 772-463-2822 for scheduling and reservation information, according to the county.

MARTY service stopped last month after the previous operator withdrew from its contract because of rising operating costs, leaving many riders without regular bus service. The county characterized the prior vendor’s action as a contract breach and said the emergency agreement would allow a phased return of public transportation.

Martin County Transit Administrator Ash Beecher said the county’s priority is to restore transportation as quickly and responsibly as possible, with particular attention to residents who rely on it for essential needs and to fiscal responsibility to taxpayers. Beecher acknowledged the disruption to riders and the broader community and said the county is working to reestablish service in a coordinated manner.

This left many people without a regular bus service. cards.headline: Flood-displaced residents press Martin County for action; warning review planned
cards.teaser: Residents demanded help at Tuesday’s commission meeting. County leaders said they plan to review the warning system and discuss a potential grant program at their next meeting.
cards.body:
Flood-displaced Martin County residents demanded action at Tuesday morning’s commission meeting, describing damaged homes and questioning the county’s response. County leaders said they plan to review the county’s warning system and revisit the flooding at their next meeting, with updates and discussion of a potential grant program.

Resident Lisa French described how the flooding had displaced her household. “Today, we’re homeless. We have nowhere to have Christmas. We don’t have much to come home to.” Jensen Beach resident Mary Berner said she had raised her family and built her life there over 40 years before watching what they had worked for become submerged in flood water and sewage.

Some residents questioned whether drainage infrastructure and development contributed to the flooding. Yamila Rollan Escalona, with the Yaya por Vida Foundation, raised concerns about response efforts. Resident Kyle Pond called on commissioners to make additional funding available to county staff that day to address the emergency.

County leaders said crews are pumping water around the clock. They also said they would explore ways to reduce future flood risks once the immediate flooding is addressed. Proposed approaches include having one agency, such as the South Florida Water Management District, manage the nearby Savannas as a single watershed and exploring additional drainage options.

Commissioner Sarah Heard addressed residents’ demands: “Jensen Beach residents, we’ve heard you loud and clear. You are our top priority.” The county’s stated plans call for a warning-system review, while the potential grant program remains a topic for discussion at the next meeting.

cards.headline: Martin County votes 3-2 to pursue quiet zones in Jensen Beach and Hobe Sound
cards.teaser: Three crossings will be the first targeted for quiet zones after commissioners reversed last year’s unanimous rejection. The approved motion narrowed an initial proposal covering all 27 railroad crossings.
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners voted 3-2 Tuesday to pursue train quiet zones at three initial crossings in Jensen Beach and Hobe Sound, reversing last year’s unanimous rejection of quiet zones amid complaints about train horns.

An initial motion called for turning all 27 railroad crossings into quiet zones. The second motion, which passed, narrowed the scope. Work will begin with two crossings at County Line Road and Skyline Drive in Jensen Beach and a third along Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound near Mariner Sands.

Opponents raised safety concerns, while supporters described train noise as a quality-of-life issue. Doug Farley, a quiet zone supporter, described the disruption from the horns.

“The horn all day and all night. And as I'm listening to that noisy disruption, I can visualize the intersection with four gates down, deployed, and cars safely behind them with that horn pointlessly bothering people,” Farley said.

Elsewhere on the Treasure Coast, St. Lucie County has established a quiet zone at three crossings in the southern end of the county. The city of Stuart recently received a $1.86 million grant to enhance rail corridor safety. In Palm Beach County, Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens recently established quiet zones.

And as I'm listening to that noisy disruption, I can visualize the intersection with four gates down, deployed, and cars safely behind them with that horn pointlessly bothering people,' said Doug Farley, a quiet zone supporter. St. Lucie County has established a quiet zone in the southern end of the county at three crossings. In Palm Beach County, both Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens recently set up quiet zones.

cards.headline: Flooding damages Terry Polk's Fort Pierce home two years after tornado loss
cards.teaser: Terry Polk said she was rescued by kayak after floodwater rose inside her Fort Pierce home. Two years after a tornado destroyed her previous home, she is unsure whether her flood insurance will cover all the repairs.
cards.body:
Heavy rain during the first weekend of November flooded Terry Polk's Fort Pierce home, leaving extensive damage two years after a Hurricane Milton tornado destroyed her previous home. Polk said she has flood insurance but is unsure whether her coverage will pay to fix everything.

Water rose to depths measured in feet inside the home as flooding swept through her block. Polk was inside when the water began rising. “We were actually in the house,” Polk said. “When we were wading around, like around knee-deep water, I started getting scared.”

Polk said she and others were rescued by kayaks and returned after the water receded. The flooding left ruined furniture and drywall, which piled up as debris in front of her home.

Two years ago, Polk lived in the Spanish Lakes community of St. Lucie County when Hurricane Milton spawned widespread tornadoes. An EF3 tornado struck the community, killing six people and destroying homes, including hers.

Her friend Cindy McGee described Polk as someone who helps those around her. “Terry is one of the most amazing people I've met,” McGee said. “She's very strong, does a lot for the community, a lot for the neighborhood.”

Facing another damaged home, Polk said she was thankful to have survived. “You know, to keep your focus, you just have to realize there are people out there that have it way worse. There are people out there that are so much worse, you know, and I have to be thankful that we got out with our lives,” she said.

"You know, to keep your focus, you just have to realize there are people out there that have it way worse. There are people out there that are so much worse, you know, and I have to be thankful that we got out with our lives," she said. One of the twisters, an EF3, struck the community, killing six people and destroying homes, including Terry's. "Terry is one of the most amazing people I've met," said friend Cindy McGee. "She's very strong, does a lot for the community, a lot for the neighborhood." hero.headline: Stuart parade, Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce ceremonies set for Veterans Day
hero.body:
Veterans Day events on Wednesday, Nov. 11, will bring parades, ceremonies and gatherings to communities across Martin, St. Lucie, Indian River, Palm Beach and Okeechobee counties. In Stuart, the Veterans Day Parade and Ceremony starts at 10 a.m. The parade will travel along East Ocean Boulevard and finish at Memorial Park. The Stuart event is among several morning observances on the regional schedule, with ceremonies in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce beginning an hour later. Indian River County’s calendar includes an evening observance and a separate gathering for veterans in Vero Beach.

Port St. Lucie’s ceremony starts at 11 a.m. at Veterans Memorial Park, 2100 S.E. Veterans Memorial Parkway. Admission is free. The program will feature music and remarks, along with a rifle salute, a flyover and Taps. With seating limited, organizers encourage visitors to get there early and take a chair. Fort Pierce also will honor veterans with an 11 a.m. ceremony at its Veterans Memorial Park. After that ceremony, VFW Post 8058 will host a free lunch with live entertainment beginning at noon. The post is at 3475 Douglas Ave. The ceremony and lunch are listed as separate parts of Fort Pierce’s Veterans Day events.

In Indian River County, the Veterans Day Observance is scheduled for 5:30 p.m. Those planning to attend should consult the county calendar for the location and further event details. The calendar also includes Veterans Meet Up, scheduled from 6 to 8 p.m. at Our House Network in Vero Beach. That event is a gathering for veterans. In Okeechobee County, a Veterans Day celebration at Okeechobee KOA RV Resort runs from 5 to 8 p.m. Central Elementary also has an 8:30 a.m. Veterans Day celebration, and the school has invited families to submit photographs of veterans.

Palm Beach County’s schedule begins with Wellington’s 8:15 a.m. parade from Village Hall, 12300 Forest Hill Blvd., followed by an 8:30 a.m. ceremony at the Wellington Veterans Memorial at Forest Hill and South Shore boulevards. Delray Beach and North Palm Beach have 9 a.m. ceremonies, while Royal Palm Beach’s event runs from 9 a.m. to noon at the Royal Palm Beach Cultural Center, 151 Civic Center Way. Palm Beach Gardens’ 11 a.m. Veterans Salute Celebration includes a keynote speaker and the Palm Beach Gardens High School Chorus. Boca Raton’s free Red, White & Boca event runs from 4 to 7 p.m. at Mizner Park Amphitheater, 590 Plaza Real, with music, speakers, a veterans marketplace and a classic car show. Lake Worth Beach’s celebration starts at 5 p.m.

hero.headline: Overflowing pond threatens at least three graves at Jensen Beach cemetery
hero.teaser: A neighboring pond overflowed onto the cemetery property during last week’s heavy rain. One family fears further flooding could cause caskets to float.
hero.body:
At least three graves are threatened by flooding at Washington Memorial Cemetery in Jensen Beach after a neighborhood pond overflowed onto the cemetery property during last week’s heavy rain. The pond borders the burial grounds, where rising water has halted burials and left families worried about loved ones already laid to rest. Allecia Dixon, a volunteer at the historic cemetery, which her family manages, said one casket has begun to sink. Families fear that as the ground takes on more water, buried caskets could move or float, creating another painful problem for people already grieving.

Henrietta Cooper had planned to bury her brother, Henry, at the cemetery over the weekend, near other members of their family. Instead, the flooding forced her to put those plans on hold. Cooper said she was stunned when she visited the grounds and saw the water. “It's unbelievable,” she said. With the burial delayed, she is considering whether she will have to find another place for her brother, despite her wish to keep him with relatives buried at Washington Memorial. “I would like for him to be here,” Cooper said. The delay has left her waiting to lay him to rest.

For Dixon and the families with relatives buried at the cemetery, the concern extends beyond when new burials can resume. Water is getting closer to some buried caskets, and Dixon fears additional flooding could leave families facing the prospect of moving their loved ones’ remains. “Our fear, potentially, is that if we have more flooding that we're going to have floating caskets,” she said. According to Dixon, that has happened once before. She said having to bury a loved one again in a different location because of the water would compound families’ grief rather than allow them to find closure.

The cemetery flooding comes as other families contend with flooded streets and damaged homes following the recent heavy rain. At Washington Memorial, those conditions have interrupted a family’s burial plans while raising concerns about the safety of existing graves. Cooper remains caught between wanting her brother buried with family and needing to move forward. “I can't wait too long,” she said. Meanwhile, Gov. Ron DeSantis has requested a major disaster declaration to help obtain federal funding for Central and South Florida communities affected by the flooding. The request comes as residents face the consequences of the high water, including the families waiting to bury loved ones in Jensen Beach.

She said it has happened once before. Now, at least three graves are at risk after a neighborhood pond that butts up against the cemetery grounds overflowed onto the property during last week’s heavy rain. Dixon said the flooding could add to families’ grief.

cards.headline: Martin County crews begin pumping process for flooded Hyline Drive
cards.body:
Martin County crews began setting up hoses on Jensen Beach Boulevard on Monday to start the process of pumping water from Hyline Pond and draining the flooded Hyline Drive area. Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said the process could take at least a week.

The county deployed two additional pumps to the area, Gorton said. Crews are pumping water out of a receiving pond so it can take water from the Hyline area. That water must then be drained from the receiving pond as part of the process, he said.
cards.article_text: And Monday, crews were setting up hoses on Jensen Beach Boulevard to begin the process of pumping water out of the Hyline Pond. Related: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall “We've deployed two additional pumps up to that area. And what we're doing is pumping out the receiving pond, because we have to move the water from the Hyline area to another pond and then drain it out of that pond,” Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said. It’s a process Gorton said could take at least a week or longer.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton and One
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council approved the site plan for a 6,000-seat soccer stadium at the “Walton and One” development area. The city plans to reimburse the developers up to $27.5 million through tax increment financing.

The stadium is expected to cost between $50 million and $80 million. When the plan was announced, the city said taxpayer funds would not be used directly.

The stadium is planned to become the home of the Port St. Lucie Sports Club in 2028, while the team is slated to begin play in the United Soccer League in March 2027. In July, representatives for Port St. Lucie SC said groundbreaking was anticipated this year, with plans targeting November.

hero.headline: Martin County deploys two more pumps to drain flooded Hyline area in Jensen Beach
hero.body:
Martin County crews have deployed two additional pumps to drain floodwater from the Hyline area in Jensen Beach, a process that could take at least a week or longer, according to Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton.

Crews were setting up hoses on Jensen Beach Boulevard on Monday to begin pumping water out of the Hyline Pond.

Gorton said crews are pumping out a receiving pond as part of the work. Water from the Hyline area must be moved to another pond and then drained from that pond, he said.
hero.article_text: And Monday, crews were setting up hoses on Jensen Beach Boulevard to begin the process of pumping water out of the Hyline Pond. And what we're doing is pumping out the receiving pond, because we have to move the water from the Hyline area to another pond and then drain it out of that pond,” Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said. It’s a process Gorton said could take at least a week or longer.
