hero.headline: Florida 'free kill' repeal opponents, DeSantis linked to $15.5 million in donations
hero.body:
Healthcare interests and lobbying organizations contributed more than $15.5 million to political committees tied to Florida lawmakers who opposed repealing a medical malpractice restriction and to Gov. Ron DeSantis, who vetoed the repeal. The contributions, made between 2017 and 2026, included more than $700,000 tied to Sen. Gayle Harrell. The restriction, which critics call Florida's “free kill” law, limits certain families' ability to recover wrongful-death damages. The records do not establish that contributions influenced votes or the veto.

More than $12 million came from hospitals, healthcare networks, physician groups, insurers, nursing homes and other healthcare interests. More than $3 million came from lobbying organizations that opposed the repeal. Committees tied to DeSantis, primarily his Florida Freedom Fund political action committee, received approximately $12.7 million since 2017, including $170,000 in the weeks and months before his veto. The contributions spanned multiple election cycles and were not necessarily connected to the repeal legislation.

Harrell, a Republican representing part of the Treasure Coast, received more than $700,000 from the groups since 2017, including $28,000 in the weeks before the vote. Sen. Tom Leek, a northeast Florida Republican, received more than $400,000 since 2024, including $15,000 in the weeks before the vote. Rep. James Buchanan, a Sarasota County Republican, received more than $300,000 since 2018, including $46,000 in the month before the vote. Four senators and six representatives voted against the bill.

The restriction's consequences extend to families such as Beth Miller's. Her only daughter, Dawn, died hours after being discharged from a hospital following gallbladder surgery. Because Dawn was older than 25, unmarried and had no children, the law prevents Miller from recovering certain wrongful-death damages in a medical malpractice lawsuit. Critics argue that the provision creates unequal accountability based on a deceased person's age and family circumstances.

State Rep. Dana Trabulsy, a Fort Pierce Republican, sponsored House Bill 6017 to remove the restriction from Florida's Wrongful Death Act. Both chambers passed it overwhelmingly, but DeSantis vetoed it in May. He argued that expanding recoverable damages without safeguards, including caps on damages and attorney fees, could increase costs for Floridians. Gov.-elect Byron Donalds said he would review the issue before deciding his position. “We're just going to sit down, take a look at the issue, and render a decision,” Donalds said.
hero.article_text: Florida lawmakers overwhelmingly voted to repeal one of the state's most controversial medical malpractice provisions earlier this year. But despite bipartisan support, the legislation never became law.Now, a WPTV investigation is following the money behind the political fight over what critics call Florida's "free kill" law — uncovering more than $15.5 million in campaign contributions from healthcare interests and lobbying groups to political committees tied to lawmakers who opposed the repeal and to Gov. Ron DeSantis, who ultimately vetoed it.In a previous investigation, WPTV introduced viewers to Beth Miller, whose only daughter, Dawn, died just hours after being discharged from the hospital following gallbladder surgery."It's on your mind, 24/7," Miller said. "We were very close, to say the least. She was my only child, my only living relative."A medical expert who reviewed Dawn's records told WPTV she should not have been discharged from the hospital. Miller said her request for an autopsy was denied, leaving her with unanswered questions about her daughter's death."I don't have an answer to this day," she said.No court has determined whether medical negligence contributed to Dawn's death.But when Miller explored her legal options, she encountered another obstacle.Because Dawn was older than 25, unmarried and had no children, Florida law prevents Miller from recovering certain wrongful-death damages in a medical malpractice lawsuit.The restriction is part of Florida's Wrongful Death Act. Critics argue it creates a disparity in accountability by limiting the damages available to certain surviving family members based on the deceased person's age and family circumstances."It's completely arbitrary," said Jordan Dulcie, a trial attorney with Searcy Denney Scarola Barnhart & Shipley.Dulce, who previously defended hospitals in medical malpractice cases, is now among the attorneys advocating for repeal."Trying to value life from the Legislature's standpoint, I think, is always improper," he said.State Rep. Dana Trabulsy, a R-Fort Pierce, sponsored House Bill 6017, legislation aimed at removing the controversial restriction from Florida's Wrongful Death Act.The proposal passed both chambers of the Florida Legislature with overwhelming support, but in May, DeSantis vetoed the bill.The governor argued that expanding the damages families could recover without additional safeguards, including caps on damages and attorney fees, could increase costs for Floridians."That imposes costs, as those costs are put through the system that helps drive the price that people pay for normal products and premiums they pay," DeSantis said.Critics of the law argue Florida remains the only state with this particular restriction on medical malpractice wrongful-death claims.Dulcie believes politics, rather than fairness, is standing in the way of reform."It's politics. That's all it is, is politics," he said. "When you look at the end of the day, no one thinks this law is fair."So WPTV examined the campaign contributions flowing to the political figures who opposed the repeal.WPTV reviewed hundreds of campaign finance records, tracking contributions made between 2017 and 2026 to political committees tied to the 10 lawmakers who voted against HB 6017 — four senators and six representatives — and DeSantis, who vetoed it.The investigation identified more than $15.5 million in contributions from healthcare interests and lobbying organizations with a stake in the debate.Of that total:More than $12 million came from hospitals, healthcare networks, physician groups, insurance companies, nursing homes and other health care interestsMore than $3 million came from lobbying organizations that opposed HB 6017 and efforts to repeal the provisionAmong the lawmakers who opposed the bill, WPTV identified several who received substantial contributions from the groups examined.Sen. Gayle Harrell, a Republican representing part of the Treasure Coast, received more than $700,000 from the tracked groups since 2017, including $28,000 in the weeks leading up to the vote.Sen. Tom Leek, a Republican from northeast Florida, received more than $400,000 since 2024, including $15,000 in the weeks before the vote.Rep. James Buchanan, a Republican from Sarasota County, received more than $300,000 since 2018, including $46,000 in the month before the vote.But the vast majority of the contributions WPTV tracked went to political committees tied to DeSantis.Those committees, primarily his Political Action Committee Florida Freedom Fund, received approximately $12.7 million since 2017, including $170,000 in the weeks and months preceding his veto.The contributions were made over multiple election cycles and were not necessarily connected to HB 6017. Campaign finance records do not establish that the money influenced any lawmaker's vote or the governor's veto.Still, Dulcie argues the financial resources available to groups opposing changes to the law create an imbalance in Tallahassee."Unfortunately, the victims of medical negligence don't have hundreds of lobbyists that they can pay millions of dollars to go to Tallahassee year after year to campaign to change this law," he said.WPTV contacted all 10 lawmakers who voted against the bill, as well as DeSantis, requesting interviews and asking about the contributions and their positions on the legislation.Despite multiple calls and emails, none responded to WPTV's requests.Dr. Aubrey Jewett, a political science professor at the University of Central Florida, said campaign contributions are an essential part of modern politics."There's an old saying that money is the mother's milk of politics," Jewett said, describing the importance of fundraising to political campaigns.He said businesses and lobbying organizations frequently contribute to politicians they believe will support their interests."I mean, it is 100% crystal clear. Most people that give are trying to get access and influence," Jewett said.But he emphasized an important distinction: political contributions alone are not evidence that a politician changed a vote or policy decision in exchange for money.Donors may support a politician because that politician already shares their views."The candidates will say, 'Well, you know, they're not like buying my vote. Instead, they support the position that I hold,'" Jewett explained.And while DeSantis vetoed HB 6017, Jewett pointed out that the governor did not rule out supporting a different version of the legislation."Gov. DeSantis did say that he would sign off on a similar bill as long as it had some caps," Jewett said.That leaves open the possibility of another attempt at repeal.With DeSantis leaving office, WPTV took the question directly to Gov.-elect Byron Donalds while he was on the campaign trail.Would he support repealing Florida's so-called "free kill" law?Donalds stopped short of committing to a position."I'm aware of Gov. DeSantis's veto on this measure. Also aware of how many members of the Legislature supported it," Donalds said. "We're just going to sit down, take a look at the issue, and render a decision. I've not made one at this time, but we're going to do what's in the best interest of the people of Florida."For families like Beth Miller's, the future of the law could determine whether others facing similar circumstances have an opportunity to seek accountability through the courts.And the debate is far from over.Since WPTV's first investigation aired, numerous viewers have reached out to share their own experiences involving alleged medical negligence and the legal barriers they encountered afterward.WPTV is continuing to investigate those cases, examine the law's impact on Florida families and seek answers from the elected

hero.headline: Martin County counts 66 flood-damaged homes, 25 destroyed, as Florida seeks federal aid
hero.body:
Flooding damaged 66 homes in Martin County, including 25 that were destroyed, according to new county figures, as Florida seeks federal disaster assistance. The state's request awaits federal approval while displaced residents in Jensen Beach contend with flooded homes and rely on neighbors, churches and community donations.

At the request of Gov. Ron DeSantis, the Florida Division of Emergency Management announced Monday that Florida had submitted a Major Disaster Declaration request for communities affected by flooding across Central and South Florida. The declaration requires federal approval before the requested assistance becomes available. Heavy rainfall left communities dealing with lingering water and damage more than a week later.

In Jensen Beach, resident Michael Drawdy described severe flooding inside his home. "Right now I've got 6 to 8 inches of water depending on the level of the house inside the house, and you can see the fecal matter that's coming through the house," Drawdy said. He and his neighbors said the conditions have made their homes unlivable.

Residents said much of their immediate help has come from one another, churches and community donations. "All these neighbors have all pulled together. They've brought us donations here every day. People have fed us from the churches. Everybody's really been really good that way," resident Suzie Keith said.

Keith said residents understand the recovery process takes time but need assistance now. "They know it's moving slowly, and we're all out of our homes, and we have nowhere to live, but they said they're doing everything they can to expedite it to FEMA," she said. Neighbors continue to rely heavily on one another as residents, businesses and local governments assess flood damage.

cards.headline: Free Bed Races return to Stuart Saturday to help Martin County families
cards.teaser: Family Promise of Martin County’s annual event runs from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Sailfish Ballpark, connecting spectators with its work to prevent and end family homelessness.
cards.body:
Family Promise of Martin County will bring its annual Bed Races back to Sailfish Ballpark in Stuart on Saturday, combining a free community event with efforts to help local families with children facing homelessness. The races are scheduled for 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the ballpark, 600 SE Flagler Ave. Paige Cortes, the organization’s director of operations, said spectators can attend for free. “So we are ready for fun too, and you can join us in the race to end childhood homelessness,” Cortes said.

Teams turn beds into racing machines, with runners pushing a rider toward the finish line. The event features costumes, competition and laughs, while giving Martin County residents an opportunity to learn about family homelessness and the work to help parents and children regain stable housing. Beyond the contest to see which team can push its bed across the finish line fastest, the races have a literal connection to Family Promise’s mission: Each bed represents something every family needs at the end of the day, a safe place to sleep.

Madeleine Bozone Greenwood, executive director of Family Promise of Martin County, said the organization works to prevent and end family homelessness locally. Its work includes homelessness prevention, shelter, transitional housing and services designed to help families find stable housing while keeping parents and children together. “We serve parents with children that are here in Martin County,” Greenwood said. “We provide shelter, transitional housing. A path to return to home ownership or their own rental housing.”

Pastor Chad Fair, board chair of Family Promise of Martin County, said homelessness affects working families, including people whose jobs involve helping local children and families. He said that reality does not always match people’s expectations about who experiences homelessness. “We kind of think that it hits just those people we see on the street corner, but it’s families, it’s nurses, it’s school teachers, it’s people that are integral in our community and do the work with our kids, with our families, and they’re experiencing homelessness,” Fair said. Saturday’s event connects residents with that sometimes largely invisible issue while highlighting efforts to help families secure stable housing.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton and One
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council approved the site plan for a 6,000-seat soccer stadium at the Walton and One development area. The stadium is expected to cost between $50 million and $80 million, with the city planning to reimburse developers up to $27.5 million through tax increment financing.

When the plan was announced, the city said taxpayer funds would not be used directly. The stadium will be home to the Port St. Lucie Sports Club starting in 2028. The team is slated to begin play in the United Soccer League in March 2027.

Representatives for Port St. Lucie SC said in July that groundbreaking for the stadium was anticipated this year, with plans targeting November.

hero.headline: Martin County counts 66 flood-damaged homes, 25 destroyed, as Florida seeks federal aid
hero.body:
Flooding has damaged 66 homes in Martin County, including 25 that were destroyed, according to new county numbers, as Florida seeks federal disaster assistance. The request awaits federal approval while displaced residents in Jensen Beach contend with flooded homes and rely on neighbors, churches and community donations.

At the request of Gov. Ron DeSantis, the Florida Division of Emergency Management announced Monday that the state had submitted a Major Disaster Declaration request for communities affected by flooding across Central and South Florida. Heavy rainfall left communities dealing with lingering water and damage more than a week later. A Major Disaster Declaration requires federal approval before the requested assistance becomes available. “We remain committed to working with our federal partners to ensure impacted Floridians receive the assistance they need to recover,” the Florida Division of Emergency Management said in a post on X.

In Jensen Beach, resident Michael Drawdy described severe flooding inside his home. He said water measured 6 to 8 inches deep, depending on the level of the house, and that fecal matter was coming through the home. Drawdy and his neighbors said the conditions had made their homes unlivable. Some residents said they were already out of their homes and struggling to determine what to do next.

Resident Suzie Keith said neighbors and churches have provided immediate help while residents wait for assistance. “All these neighbors have all pulled together. They've brought us donations here every day. People have fed us from the churches. Everybody's really been really good that way,” Keith said. She said residents understand the recovery process takes time but need assistance now, with people displaced from their homes. Neighbors continue to rely heavily on one another, she said.

hero.headline: Flooding threatens at least three graves at Jensen Beach cemetery
hero.teaser: A neighboring pond overflowed onto the cemetery grounds during last week’s heavy rain. A family fears further flooding could cause caskets to float.
hero.body:
At least three graves are threatened by flooding at Washington Memorial Cemetery in Jensen Beach after a nearby neighborhood pond overflowed during last week’s heavy rain. The pond lies next to the cemetery, allowing water to spread onto the burial grounds. Burials have been suspended, leaving some families unable to lay their loved ones to rest. Water is also approaching some caskets already buried there. Families are concerned that increasingly saturated ground could allow caskets to move or float, adding another burden as they grieve and raising fears about what further flooding could mean for the cemetery.

Henrietta Cooper had intended to bury her brother, Henry, at the cemetery over the weekend, near other members of their family. Those arrangements were put on hold because of the floodwater. Cooper said she was shocked when she visited the grounds. “I came this way yesterday,” she said. “I looked at it and said, ‘Wow.’ It’s unbelievable.” With the burial delayed, she is considering whether she will have to choose another cemetery, despite wanting her brother to remain with their relatives. “I may have to find some other place to put him but all our family’s here,” Cooper said. “I would like for him to be here.”

Allecia Dixon, a volunteer whose family manages the historic cemetery, said one casket has already begun to sink. Her family is worried that additional flooding could create a more serious problem for those buried on the property. “Our fear, potentially, is that if we have more flooding that we’re going to have floating caskets,” Dixon said. She said that had happened once before. The threat now extends to at least three graves affected by water from the overflowing pond. For families with relatives buried there, the concern goes beyond the current water levels to the possibility that loved ones might have to be buried again elsewhere.

Dixon said having to relocate a loved one’s remains because of flooding could compound the pain of families seeking closure after a death. Cooper, meanwhile, remains unable to complete the burial she had planned for her brother. “I can’t wait too long,” she said. The cemetery’s problems come as other families in flood-hit communities cope with inundated streets and damage to their homes. Gov. Ron DeSantis has requested a major disaster declaration to help obtain federal funding for Central and South Florida following the historic flooding. At the cemetery, families are still facing both postponed burials and concerns about existing graves.

Dixon said the flooding could add to families’ grief.

cards.headline: Martin County deploys two more pumps to drain flooded Hyline area
cards.body:
Martin County has deployed two additional pumps to help drain floodwaters from the Hyline area, according to county Public Works Director Jim Gorton. He said the process could take at least a week or longer.

Crews were setting up hoses on Jensen Beach Boulevard on Monday to begin pumping water out of the Hyline Pond.

Gorton said crews are pumping out a receiving pond as part of the drainage process. Water from the Hyline area must be moved to another pond before it can be drained from that pond.

“We've deployed two additional pumps up to that area. And what we're doing is pumping out the receiving pond, because we have to move the water from the Hyline area to another pond and then drain it out of that pond,” Gorton said.

hero.headline: Martin County commissioners to review quiet-zone safety and crossing improvements Tuesday
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners are scheduled to revisit residents’ calls for train quiet zones Tuesday at 10:30 a.m., with a review of safety requirements and potential crossing improvements along the Florida East Coast Railway. Quiet zones would eliminate the requirement for trains to routinely sound their horns at designated crossings that meet federal safety requirements. Engineers could still sound their horns when necessary for safety.

Public Works staff will present an update on the Railroad Safety Capital Improvement Program and the county’s evaluation of establishing one or more quiet zones. The presentation will outline potential benefits and risks, along with the safety requirements and improvements needed to establish quiet zones in Martin County. Commissioners are expected to discuss the findings and give staff direction on how to proceed.

The review follows two earlier commission discussions. At a March 11, 2025, meeting, commissioners decided not to pursue quiet zones after reviewing options presented by county staff. Continued concerns from residents brought the issue back before commissioners in May 2026, when they directed staff to continue evaluating the possibility.

Brightline began commercial operations along the Florida East Coast Railway through the Treasure Coast in September 2023, adding approximately 32 daily train trips through the corridor. The increased traffic prompted residents to press county leaders to explore quiet zones. Hobe Sound resident Glenn Malone supports reducing horn use while preserving engineers’ ability to sound warnings for safety. Fellow Hobe Sound resident Jeffry Aderman raised concerns about the noise: “We don’t have a problem with that. We just don’t want the inherent noise all day and night long,” he said.

Quiet zones would eliminate the requirement for trains to routinely sound their horns at designated crossings, provided those crossings meet federal safety requirements. Train engineers would still be able to sound their horns when necessary for safety. For neighbors living near the tracks, the issue comes down to finding a balance between safety and quality of life. hero.headline: FHP investigates fatal SUV-motorcycle crash on 37th Street in Indian River County
hero.body:
Florida Highway Patrol is investigating a collision between an SUV and a motorcycle that killed a 58-year-old man Monday afternoon on 37th Street in unincorporated Indian River County. The crash occurred around 3:43 p.m. near 1850 37th Street.

According to FHP, an 82-year-old woman driving a 2018 Toyota Rav 4 SUV was heading east on 37th Street when she stopped in the roadway to wait to turn left into Indian River MRI. The SUV then turned into the path of an approaching westbound 2017 Harley Davidson Electra Guide Motorcycle, and the vehicles collided, FHP said.

The motorcycle’s driver, a 58-year-old man, was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where he was pronounced dead. The woman driving the SUV suffered minor injuries.

The crash prompted the closure of westbound 37th Street between U.S. Highway 1 and 17th Avenue. FHP described the investigation as active.

hero.headline: Western St. Lucie County flooding prompts emergency meeting, push for faster study
hero.body:
The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday after last week’s flooding submerged homes, farms and roads in western St. Lucie County. Later Monday, Port St. Lucie Councilman David Pickett urged the city to accelerate a stormwater study planned for 2029.

Farmers, residents and representatives of Save the Chimps attended the district meeting to seek answers and long-term drainage solutions. District President Steve Cassens said the existing system has limits during extreme rainfall. “We can manage water maybe 3, 4, 5, 6 inches. We can’t manage water in the quantities that we got.” District officials discussed examining engineering options as part of a possible long-range plan. They also addressed waterway and ditch maintenance, including concerns about a creek in Western Fort Pierce that serves as a primary drainage route. The district said it systematically cleans ditches within its boundaries.

At Monday’s Port St. Lucie City Council meeting, Pickett said he had sent two memos to the city manager addressing floodwaters and wanted the stormwater study expedited rather than waiting until 2029. He also raised concerns about flooding in Tradition and called for examining stormwater systems before distributing certain stormwater fees to community development districts.

Justin Akerley, who helps operate Saint Lucie Farm Preserve in west Fort Pierce, attended both meetings. He told council members he believes continued development is adding pressure to drainage infrastructure and urged city leaders to reconsider development’s effects on flooding. “I’ve got friends that have calves dying that are flooded, they can’t get out,” he said. “It’s a terrible, terrible situation for everybody. There’s people that have lost their homes.” Akerley and Michael Hale operate the working agritourism farm, which produces hay, cut flowers, beef and assorted vegetables. The farm also hosts community agricultural events.

Conditions had significantly improved at Save the Chimps, a sanctuary in western St. Lucie County where staff used drones to deliver food to chimpanzees while several roads were underwater. “A short 40 hours after that, we’re almost completely dry on our roads,” Mark Yohannan said. Residents and farmers at Monday’s district meeting sought ways to reduce the risk of similar flooding during another extreme rainfall event.

hero.headline: Martin County commissioners to review safety requirements for train quiet zones
hero.teaser: A 10:30 a.m. presentation Tuesday will examine potential quiet-zone benefits, risks and crossing improvements following continued pressure from residents.
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners are scheduled to review safety requirements and potential improvements Tuesday morning for proposed railroad quiet zones, which would end routine train horn requirements at designated crossings. The review follows continued pressure from residents seeking relief from train noise along the Florida East Coast Railway.

Public Works staff is scheduled to present an update at 10:30 a.m. on the Railroad Safety Capital Improvement Program and the county’s evaluation of establishing one or more quiet zones. The presentation will outline potential risks and benefits, along with the safety requirements and improvements needed to establish the zones. Commissioners are expected to discuss the findings and give staff direction on how to proceed.

Crossings would have to meet federal safety requirements before quiet zones could be established. Train engineers would retain the ability to sound their horns when necessary for safety. Hobe Sound resident Glenn Malone supports reducing horn noise while preserving engineers’ ability to use the horn for safety. Another Hobe Sound resident, Jeffry Aderman, has raised concerns about train noise throughout the day and night.

Brightline began commercial operations along the Florida East Coast Railway through the Treasure Coast in September 2023, adding approximately 32 daily train trips through the corridor. The increased rail traffic prompted residents to call on county leaders to explore quiet zones.

Commissioners decided against pursuing quiet zones at a March 11, 2025, meeting after reviewing options presented by county staff. Following continued resident concerns, they revisited the issue in May 2026 and directed staff to continue evaluating the possibility. Tuesday’s scheduled presentation continues that evaluation.

Train engineers would still be able to sound their horns when necessary for safety.For neighbors living near the tracks, the issue comes down to finding a balance between safety and quality of life."Safety considerations may not be as important, but they need to have the ability to sound that horn," said Glenn Malone of Hobe Sound, "If they can regulate it down just a bit so the option for safety is still viable."Brightline began commercial operations along the Florida East Coast Railway through the Treasure Coast in September 2023, adding approximately 32 daily train trips through the corridor.The increased rail traffic prompted residents to call on county leaders to explore quiet zones."We don’t have a problem with that. cards.headline: Martin County crews begin pumping process for flooded Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach
cards.body:
Martin County crews began preparations Monday to pump water from the flooded Hyline Drive area in Jensen Beach, deploying two additional pumps for a process that could take at least a week or longer, according to Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton.

Crews were setting up hoses on Jensen Beach Boulevard to begin pumping water out of the Hyline Pond.

Gorton said crews are pumping out a receiving pond as part of the drainage process. Water from the Hyline area must be moved to another pond and then drained from that pond, he said.

hero.headline: Flooding leaves Greene Sugars Farm groves in Vero Beach underwater for over a week
hero.body:
Citrus groves at Greene Sugars Farm in Vero Beach have been underwater for more than a week despite pumping every morning and night. Flooding from last week’s heavy rain has put crops, trees and livestock in jeopardy at the multigenerational, family-owned operation.

Aubrey Greene said the farm received more than 10 inches of rain in a single night. Water has flooded the groves from trunk to trunk, with heavy pumping twice a day as the flooding persists.

Greene Sugars Farm has 800 acres of lemon trees, 50 acres of sugar belle trees and thousands of cattle. The farm produces roughly 60,000 to 80,000 boxes of citrus each year and has a contract with Coca-Cola.

Greene said the farm had a great citrus season last year and had anticipated another good year before the flooding threatened the operation’s crops, trees and livestock.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie council approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton & One
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council approved a site plan Monday for a proposed 6,000-seat soccer stadium on city-owned land at Walton & One, near U.S. 1, SE Village Green Drive and Walton Road. The project still has outstanding requirements involving water and sewer service, drainage plans and public art. City staff recommended approval subject to recording a replat. The city is also advancing zoning and sign-program changes to allow the stadium and its taller lights and scoreboard. Those measures were listed on Monday’s agenda for second reading.

Traffic planning and potential public reimbursement are also part of the project. The site-plan review included a traffic analysis and a special-event traffic plan reviewed by police and Public Works. Residents have previously raised concerns about traffic near the proposed site. Event parking would use other city-owned parcels under a parking license in the operating arrangement. The city says the project will not use money from its general fund. Under the city’s published terms, the developer could receive reimbursement for up to 50% of eligible stadium and infrastructure costs through community redevelopment agency tax-increment revenue, capped at $27.5 million.

The approved plan calls for seven buildings totaling 133,412 square feet, including the stadium, a cabana, concession and restroom facilities, and three retail buildings. Development is planned in four phases, starting with the approximately 97,296-square-foot, two-story stadium, followed by the retail buildings. The stadium would stand 61 feet tall. Its LED scoreboard could reach 85 feet, and field-light poles could rise to 135 feet.

The stadium is planned as the home of Port St. Lucie SC, a United Soccer League League One team expected to begin play in 2027. Matches at the new stadium are planned to begin in 2028. The venue is also intended to host concerts, festivals and other events. It is part of the broader Walton & One redevelopment, envisioned as a mix of residential, retail, office, hotel and entertainment uses. The city says it acquired 22 parcels in the district in 2022 and intends the stadium to help spur development there.

cards.headline: Receding floodwaters restore access at Save the Chimps in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: Staff can drive on about 90% of the sanctuary’s roads after 19 inches of rain flooded the property. Workers are using tractors, trailers and large off-road vehicles as care operations recover.
cards.body:
Receding floodwaters have restored access to most roads at Save the Chimps in Fort Pierce after 19 inches of rain flooded the 150-acre sanctuary and disrupted care for its 211 rescued chimpanzees. Staff are relying on tractors, trailers and large off-road vehicles to move around the property after flooding sidelined golf carts and damaged some of them.

Mark Yohannan, facilities director at Save the Chimps, said water levels had dropped significantly, making about 90% of the sanctuary’s 1.2 miles of roads visible and drivable. “We've probably lost at least 7 or 8 inches of water,” Yohannan said. He expected the remaining stretch of road to dry overnight. An overflowing header canal has slowed the water’s recession. On Monday, Yohannan met with the St. Lucie Water River District to discuss the flooding. He described the rainfall as a 200-year event and said the county was working to get water moving.

Before the water began receding, staff used a drone to deliver food to Caleb, a chimpanzee who stayed on his island. Ana Paula Tavares, CEO of Save the Chimps, said Caleb remained outside until flooding covered the land bridge connecting his island to his indoor house, preventing him from going inside. The sanctuary has 12 islands, each housing a family group of 11 to 21 chimpanzees, with care houses on higher ground. Tavares said the flooded connection prompted staff to find a creative way to get Caleb food and fluids.

Flooding also complicated the daily movement of staff and 3,000 pounds of food around the sanctuary. Yohannan said care staff normally use battery-powered golf carts, but submerged roads made those vehicles unusable, and some carts sustained damage. Sanctuary leaders said they felt mostly prepared for the flooding while identifying areas for improvement. Tavares said the experience prompted plans to look into flood insurance. Yohannan said very large pumps would have been needed and that closer attention to the forecast might have helped. He compared the sanctuary’s situation with that of its neighbors facing the same unusually heavy rainfall.
cards.article_text: Save the Chimps, a 150-acre chimpanzee sanctuary in Fort Pierce, is recovering after 19 inches of rain caused historic flooding, disrupting operations and making it difficult for staff to care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. Mark Yohannan, facilities director at Save the Chimps, said water levels have dropped significantly, allowing staff to regain access to most of the sanctuary’s roads. "We've probably lost at least 7 or 8 inches of water. Now we have 1.2 miles of road here on property, 90% of that we can actually see and drive on. We expect the last little bit to dry up overnight," Yohannan said. Before the water began receding, staff faced challenges, including delivering food to a chimpanzee via drone. The sanctuary has 12 islands that house 11-21 chimpanzees in a family group. In total, there are 211 chimpanzees on the property. "We saw that we had a situation. Caleb was the one that stayed out; he loves his island as many others do," said Ana Paula Tavares, CEO of Save the Chimps. "He decided he was going to stay out until he realized that he was not going to be able to go indoors anymore because of the land bridge that connects the island to his indoor house got flooded as well. Not on all the islands, but on that island. That's when we had to get creative and think, how can we drop fluid and food?" The sanctuary’s chimps live on islands with care houses situated on higher ground, but staff struggled to navigate the flooded property. "We have a lot of golf carts that care staff use to move themselves, staff, 3,000 pounds of food a day, and so, those were rendered inoperable because you couldn't see the road; they're battery carts... Not to mention some were damaged," Yohannan said. Employees have been relying on tractors, trailers, and large off-road vehicles to access the sanctuary. An overflowing header canal has slowed the water’s recession. On Monday, Yohannan met with the St. Lucie Water River District to discuss the flooding. "We left with the understanding that everyone already knows. This rain event was a 200-year event, and I think that the county's working as hard as they can to get stuff moving," Yohannan said. Despite the historic flood, rescue leaders felt they were mostly prepared but acknowledged areas for improvement. "The one thing that came to mind is we have insurance...very good insurance but not flood insurance because we didn't have floods in Florida. So now we do, or now we will look into that...that was one lesson learned," Tavares said. Yohannan added, "We would have needed some very large pumps, watched the forecast a little better maybe...but other than that I think we're in the same boat as all the other neighbors. It's the first thing that's rained this hard in 200 years; I don't know what we could've done to be more prepared." cards.headline: St. Lucie County schools set to reopen Monday after flooding; bus stops may change
cards.teaser: The district announced plans to reopen all schools Monday, Nov. 9. Some bus stops may temporarily move because of road conditions, and recovery resources include government assistance information.
cards.body:
The school district in St. Lucie County announced plans to reopen all schools Monday, Nov. 9, after historic flooding across the county. Most bus stops will operate as usual, but some may be temporarily relocated because of road conditions, the district said.

The district said families with affected stops would receive a call from the SLPS Transportation Department on Sunday. Families who do not receive a call will keep their child’s regular stop. hero.headline: Cape Coral man arrested on Martin County warrant over alleged online threats
hero.teaser: Michael Davis is accused of threatening local law enforcement and a family, including a former Felix Williams Elementary School student. Investigators are pursuing leads that could bring additional charges.
hero.body:
Michael Davis, a Cape Coral resident accused of posting online threats against law enforcement officers and a Martin County family, was arrested on a Martin County warrant and booked into the Lee County Jail on a $100,000 bond, according to Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. The sheriff said Davis made several TikTok videos containing threats and references to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office, Stuart Police and a child who previously attended Felix Williams Elementary School. “This individual or suspect was threatening to kill or shoot any pig or police officer that came upon him or came near him,” Budensiek said.

Budensiek said the threats were directed at both police officers and the family, including the former elementary school student. The child mentioned in the videos no longer attends Felix Williams Elementary. The sheriff said the references to local law enforcement and the family prompted investigators to examine Davis’ connection to Martin County. “You don’t ever threaten our deputies. You don’t threaten the citizens of Martin County. You certainly don’t threaten our youth and expect us just to sit on our worlds and not take action,” Budensiek said. Authorities are continuing to investigate the alleged threats and pursue leads that could support additional charges.

Davis appears to have lived in Martin County from 2006 to 2014, according to Budensiek. The sheriff said Davis claims he had a fight with the family he is accused of threatening, but the family does not remember him or the incident he described. “The question we had is why is he fixated on Martin County? Why is he fixated on this family?” Budensiek said. He said investigators had not resolved that connection. “They have no idea who this guy is. They don’t know of an incident that happened at the beach. They are as confused as we are trying to make these connections,” he said.

Budensiek also said Davis does not appear to have a criminal record or a history of mental health issues. He expressed concern for parents, especially those with children in school, while discussing the bond and investigators’ efforts to develop further cases. “I was hoping that $100,000 bond, he would still be sitting in jail and our parents, especially our school parents, wouldn’t have to worry. Just know this so that we are working diligently to come up with other cases and other charges that may change that. But we are not there yet,” Budensiek said.

cards.body:

Crews were setting up hoses on Jensen Beach Boulevard on Monday to begin pumping water out of the Hyline Pond. Gorton said the process could take at least a week or longer.

The work requires moving water in stages. Crews are pumping out a receiving pond so water from the Hyline area can be moved into it and then drained from that pond, Gorton said.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton & One
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved a site plan Monday for a proposed 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton & One, advancing the redevelopment near U.S. 1, SE Village Green Drive and Walton Road. The council held a brief discussion before approving the plan, which calls for seven buildings totaling 133,412 square feet on city-owned land. The stadium is intended to anchor a broader redevelopment envisioned to include residential, retail, office, hotel and entertainment uses.

The project still has outstanding requirements involving water and sewer service, drainage plans and public art. Staff recommended site-plan approval subject to recording a replat. The city says the project will not use money from its general fund. Under the city’s published project terms, the developer could receive reimbursement for up to 50% of eligible stadium and infrastructure costs through community redevelopment agency tax-increment revenue, capped at $27.5 million. The site-plan review also included a traffic analysis and a special-event traffic plan reviewed by police and Public Works. Residents have previously raised concerns about traffic near the proposed site.

The development would include the stadium, a cabana, concession and restroom facilities, and three retail buildings. Construction is planned in four phases, beginning with the approximately 97,296-square-foot, two-story stadium, followed by the retail buildings. The stadium would stand 61 feet tall, with an LED scoreboard that could reach 85 feet and field-light poles that could rise to 135 feet. The city is also advancing related zoning and sign-program changes to allow the stadium and its taller lights and scoreboard. Those measures were listed on Monday’s agenda for second reading.

The stadium is planned as the home of Port St. Lucie SC, a United Soccer League League One team expected to begin play in 2027. Matches at the new stadium are planned to begin in 2028, and the venue is also intended to host concerts, festivals and other events. The city says it acquired 22 parcels in the Walton & One district in 2022 and intends for the stadium to help spur development there. Parking for stadium events would use other city-owned parcels under a parking license in the operating arrangement.

cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue said an accidental electrical issue caused Saturday morning’s fire on N.W. Charlie Green Drive. Firefighters contained the flames before they spread to a nearby home.
cards.body:
An accidental electrical issue caused an RV fire that killed a family dog Saturday morning in Jensen Beach, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. Firefighters quickly contained the flames, preventing them from spreading to a nearby home.

Multiple units from Martin County Fire Rescue and Stuart Fire Rescue responded to the 1200 block of N.W. Charlie Green Drive. Crews arrived to find a 20-foot camper fully engulfed in flames near the back of a house and worked together to extinguish the fire.

The family dog died despite firefighters’ efforts, Martin County Fire Rescue said. Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies and Animal Control officers also responded.

hero.headline: Florida homeowners hit by flooding may qualify for partial property tax refunds
hero.body:
Florida homeowners affected by last week's flooding may qualify for a partial property tax refund if their residences are uninhabitable for at least 30 consecutive days. Florida law allows the refunds when a catastrophic event leaves a residence uninhabitable for that period, according to Palm Beach County Appraiser Dorothy Jacks.

Homeowners seeking the refund must submit an Application for Catastrophic Event Tax Refund, Form DR-465, along with supporting documentation by March 1, 2027. The application and documentation are required for homeowners seeking a refund for damage.

Damage from this flooding will not change a property's 2026 assessment. It may affect the property's 2027 assessment if repairs remain incomplete as of Jan. 1, 2027. That assessment date is separate from the March 1 deadline to apply for a catastrophic event tax refund.

Flooding from last week's heavy rains persists in some areas of South Florida and the Treasure Coast. At the Grand Isles condos off Haverhill Road in West Palm Beach, water around resident Jesse Cabral's condo remains more than ankle-deep and reaches his garage. Cabral said the flooding caused extensive damage inside the garage. “It's been a definite challenge,” he said.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie cooking class teaches adults with disabilities skills for independence
hero.body:
Adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities practiced meal preparation and kitchen safety during an October cooking class in Port St. Lucie designed to help them become more independent. With Mediterranean chicken on the menu, participants chopped vegetables, prepared ingredients and followed a recipe to make a healthier meal.

The participants are part of the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County’s Guardian Advocacy Program, which provides guardianship support to people with developmental disabilities. Some are young adults who have aged out of foster care. Through a partnership with GL Homes that has lasted nearly a decade, participants receive hands-on experiences and opportunities to develop everyday skills.

Organizers say the goal is to help participants become more self-sufficient while giving them opportunities that are often difficult for them to access. “We wanted to give them these experiences that they just don't have and the rest of us take for granted,” said Sarah Alsofrom, Vice President of Community Relations at GL Homes. Jessica Kelson with the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County said learning new skills and participating in activities can make a meaningful difference. “Being able to watch them learn a new skill or participate in something that's not typically offered to them is just really heartwarming and nice to see them be able to grow,” Kelson said.

By the end of the class, participants had prepared their meal and sat down to eat what they made. One participant expressed pride in the accomplishment and a desire to use her new skills at home. “I'm proud of it,” she said. “I am going to try this at home.”

hero.headline: Martin County schools to get more deputies after threat suspect posts $100,000 bond
hero.body:
A Cape Coral man accused of making TikTok threats against Felix A. Williams Elementary School in Stuart, law enforcement officers and Martin County community members was released from the Lee County Jail on Sunday after posting a $100,000 bond. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it will increase deputy presence at and around the elementary school and at several other Martin County schools as a precaution following the release of Michael G. Davis, 51.

Felix A. Williams Elementary School will remain open, and teaching and learning will continue as planned, Principal Sarah Tuthill said in a statement posted to the school’s Facebook page Sunday night. Tuthill said the sheriff’s office continues to monitor the situation closely and is coordinating with the school on the increased law enforcement presence.

Davis was arrested Saturday night in Cape Coral on a Martin County warrant directly related to the threats, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. A concerned citizen contacted the agency Friday, Nov. 6, about a TikTok video threatening the lives of a local student, community members and Martin County law enforcement officers. Investigators reviewed the threats and identified Davis as the person who posted the video, the agency said.

The sheriff’s office’s criminal investigations division and warrants unit worked with the U.S. Marshals Service and the Cape Coral Police Department to arrest Davis. He initially refused to surrender to officers outside his home before being taken into custody, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. The Lee County Sheriff’s Office listed a charge of resisting officers without violence along with the out-of-county warrant from Martin County.

“We know parents are concerned about his release,” the Martin County Sheriff’s Office said in its Facebook post. The agency said Davis uses a bicycle as his primary form of transportation and asked anyone who thinks they see him in Martin County or notices suspicious activity to call the sheriff’s office.

hero.headline: Jensen Beach residents remain displaced as Martin County works on temporary housing
hero.body:
Residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach remain displaced a week after historic rainfall flooded their homes, while Martin County officials work to arrange temporary housing. Standing water continues to affect homes in the neighborhood, where residents brought their concerns directly to county leaders Sunday.

District 1 County Commissioner Eileen Vargas said Habitat for Humanity and United Way were working on shelter and other assistance. Jim Gorton of Martin County Public Works said temporary housing arrangements were being pursued and urged residents to make sure their contact information was available. County officials also said crews were addressing flooding concerns and evaluating whether local watersheds have enough capacity to handle floodwaters.

Lisa French, a resident of Skyline Heights, said her family left after water began approaching the house Tuesday and backing up through toilets and showers. When they returned Wednesday, water had entered the home. French said sewage-contaminated water remained inside, with fecal matter and strong odors. She described lifted flooring and said her husband had cut into walls to determine how high moisture had reached. “It's like a total teardown; we had people come, and everything in there has been sewer water sitting in hot heat,” French said.

The affected neighborhood is near the Savannas Preserve, where water naturally flows south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. French attributed the flooding in her neighborhood to water being pumped into the preserve, saying that was the explanation officials had given her. County officials described their work as addressing flooding concerns and assessing watershed capacity. French also said she and her neighbors did not have flood insurance because the area was not designated as a flood zone.

French said emergency services, local and federal leaders, and others were reaching out to help her family. She hopes to rebuild and remain on the property, even as the displacement disrupts holiday plans. “The first thing you think of is Thanksgiving is coming up; we’re supposed to host Thanksgiving. Then I’m supposed to do Christmas for my boys, and we don’t have a home… It’s just hard,” French said.

"Tuesday you can kind of see the water creep towards the house, and then we started having water come out of our toilets and our showers, so we decided to leave. Wednesday, we got back here, and there’s flooding inside the house, and this all came," French said. The affected neighborhood is located near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water naturally flows south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. French said officials explained that flooding in her area is caused by water being pumped into the Savannas Preserve from Port St. "We're at level with the Savannas, so if they try to pump, it's like how they explain it is they, they're pumping us and the Savannas at the same time," French said. Lucie, they can dump all their water from their streets into the Savanna Preserve, and it's going to come down to us." French said no one in her neighborhood, including herself, had flood insurance because the area is not designated as a flood zone. As the days went on, her home became inundated with water, and now fecal matter is floating around the house, creating strong odors. "It's like a total teardown; we had people come, and everything in there has been sewer water sitting in hot heat," French said. "Right now, it’s like a hot box because there’s sewer water 4-6 inches high everywhere. My floors are up… my husband was cutting out the walls to see how far the moisture got up. It’s gross inside; we can’t go inside anymore." District 1 County Commissioner Eileen Vargas said, "Habitat for Humanity is working with United Way right now for a shelter... plus other help." Jim Gorton, Martin County Public Works, added, "We are working on temporary housing... Make sure you have your contact information out there; next week is tomorrow. So that's being worked on." French said while emergency services, resources, and local and federal leaders are reaching out to help her family, she hopes to rebuild her home and return to normalcy. "The first thing you think of is Thanksgiving is coming up; we’re supposed to host Thanksgiving. Then I’m supposed to do Christmas for my boys, and we don’t have a home… It’s just hard," French said. hero.headline: Jensen Beach families remain stranded by flooding as county offers no relief timeline
hero.body:
Some Jensen Beach families remain stranded by deep floodwater eight days after historic rainfall, and county officials told residents at a Sunday flood relief meeting they do not know when the water will recede. Homeowners along Hyline Drive estimate water remains as high as five feet in some areas.

Residents say the standing water is mixed with sewage because many homes in the neighborhood rely on septic systems. Homeowner Todd Doss and his partner, Susan Boeve, step across concrete cinder blocks to reach their front door. Like many neighbors, they say they cannot move their cars, take showers or flush their toilets. “The smell is bad,” Doss said. “It has been very uncomfortable, but we're managing. It's kind of like camping.”

Doss, who has lived in the neighborhood for more than two decades, said some neighbors have lost everything inside their homes. Water has entered his Florida room and spilled into his pool. cards.headline: Cape Coral man arrested over alleged TikTok threats targeting Martin County
cards.teaser: Investigators say Micheal George Davis, 51, posted videos threatening a student, a school, community members and law enforcement officers. He was arrested Saturday night at his Cape Coral home.
cards.body:
A Cape Coral man was arrested Saturday night after posting TikTok videos threatening a Martin County student, a school, community members and law enforcement officers, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. Investigators identified the man as 51-year-old Micheal George Davis. His motive remains under investigation.

A concerned resident alerted the sheriff’s office late Friday about the first video. Investigators reviewed the threats, identified Davis as the person who posted them and tracked him to Cape Coral, the agency said.

The sheriff’s office Criminal Investigations Division and Warrants Unit worked with the U.S. Marshals Fugitive Task Force and Cape Coral police to arrest Davis at his home. Davis initially refused to come outside but was ultimately taken into custody on a Martin County warrant with a $100,000 bond, according to the sheriff’s office. He was also arrested for resisting arrest, according to booking records.

Sheriff John Budensiek said the agency would use every investigative resource available to identify, find and arrest anyone who threatens students, schools, community members or law enforcement officers.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Public Schools to reopen Monday, with some bus stops subject to change
hero.body:
St. Lucie Public Schools will reopen all schools Monday, Nov. 9, after historic flooding across the county. Most bus stops will operate as usual, but some may be temporarily relocated because of road conditions, the district said.

Families whose stops are affected will receive a call from the SLPS Transportation Department on Sunday. The district said a family’s regular stop remains unchanged unless it receives a call.

The district’s superintendent thanked families for their patience and praised bus drivers and school staff who worked beyond their usual hours to help students get home safely. The district has also posted recovery resources for families affected by flooding, including information about government assistance.

cards.headline: Brightline train strikes, kills pedestrian north of Walton Road in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: Deputies responded Sunday afternoon to the tracks near Savannas Preserve State Park. The sheriff's office is investigating the circumstances of the fatal strike.
cards.body:
A Brightline train struck and killed a pedestrian Sunday afternoon on railroad tracks about a mile north of Walton Road in St. Lucie County, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. Deputies responded at approximately 1:10 p.m. to a report that a pedestrian had been struck near Savannas Preserve State Park. The tracks run east of U.S. 1 and are operated by Florida East Coast Railway. Freight trains also use the route.

Preliminary information indicates that the northbound train struck a person who entered the path of the approaching train, according to a sheriff’s office spokesman. The circumstances surrounding the fatal strike remain under investigation. Some other northbound trains were affected. “Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the victim’s family and friends during this difficult time,” the sheriff’s office said.

Brightline operates passenger trains between Miami and Orlando, with maximum operating speeds that vary by track segment. Its trains reach maximum operating speeds of 110 mph between West Palm Beach and Cocoa and up to 125 mph on the dedicated track between Cocoa and Orlando International Airport. On the segment between Miami and West Palm Beach, the maximum operating speed is 79 mph. The source information did not establish the train’s speed at the time of the fatal strike.

The private company extended its service from West Palm Beach to a new station at Orlando International Airport. There are no train stations between West Palm Beach and Orlando. Plans call for a Brightline station in downtown Stuart, though that project faces significant funding and operational hurdles.

hero.headline: Jensen Beach families seek county flood relief as Hyline Drive remains underwater
hero.body:
County officials told Jensen Beach residents at a flood-relief meeting Sunday that they could not predict when standing water would recede from Hyline Drive, where families remain stranded eight days after historic rainfall flooded Treasure Coast communities.

Homeowners estimate the water remains as deep as five feet in parts of the neighborhood. Residents say it is mixed with sewage because many homes rely on septic systems. Some families say they cannot move their cars, take showers or flush their toilets. Homeowner Todd Doss and his partner, Susan Boeve, reach their front door by carefully stepping across concrete cinder blocks to avoid the water.

Doss, who has lived in the neighborhood for more than two decades, said the flooding has left some neighbors with three to four feet of water inside their homes. He has kept floodwater out of his home, though water has entered his Florida room and spilled into his pool. “The smell is bad,” Doss said. “It has been very uncomfortable, but we're managing. It's kind of like camping.” Leaving is not an option for the family, which includes two dogs, a cat and a pet tortoise named Walter.

Residents gathered with county leaders Sunday hoping to learn when conditions might improve. Some homeowners fear the flooding could take months to subside because there is nowhere to put the water. Homeowner Mike Bresette said the neighborhood has flooded before and argued that drainage improvements should have been made years ago. “They've had since 2011 to make changes to the infrastructure for drainage and no one's done anything,” Bresette said.

Doss said the water initially began draining after the rain stopped, then rose higher the next morning. He worries about another storm before the standing water disappears. “If we have one more bad rain, we will definitely be flooded,” he said.

The neighborhood is outside a designated flood zone, and many homeowners do not carry flood insurance. Florida has declared a state of emergency that includes Martin County. Homeowners say they hope the governor requests a federal disaster declaration that could allow FEMA to provide assistance.

cards.headline: Two men arrested in theft of 34 light poles from Fort Pierce property
cards.teaser: Deputies said the aluminum poles were worth $6,800 and were taken while St. Lucie County was under a flooding emergency. Investigators tracked the suspects’ truck and stopped it on Okeechobee Road.
cards.body:
Two men were arrested Friday after deputies said they stole 34 aluminum light poles worth $6,800 from a Fort Pierce property while St. Lucie County was under a state of emergency due to flooding.

Deputies and the South Florida Criminal Apprehension Team investigated suspicious activity Friday night at a property in the 3500 block of Eleven Mile Road, according to the sheriff’s office. With help from the Fort Pierce Police Department, investigators used a drone to confirm that two people were removing property and loading it into a truck. Deputies tracked the truck as it left the area and stopped it on Okeechobee Road.

The suspects, identified as Pablo Rojas Castro, 33, of Pembroke Pines, and Alberto Guia Hernandez, 35, of Miami, were taken into custody without incident, the sheriff’s office said. Investigators valued the stolen aluminum light poles at $6,800.

Castro and Hernandez face charges of burglary of an unoccupied dwelling during a state of emergency, traveling across county lines to commit burglary, grand theft during a state of emergency and possession of burglary tools. The arrests came during the county’s state of emergency following flooding that week.

hero.headline: Trailside flooding crowds Hungryland Farms cattle onto high ground in Martin County
hero.body:
Flooding in Martin County’s Trailside community has displaced Hungryland Farms’ cattle onto limited high ground and affected neighboring ranches and properties. Repairs to a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal are awaiting lower water levels and safe access, according to the county.

Much of the pasture at Hungryland Farms is underwater, leaving the herd crowded onto the elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico said. The flooding has cut off much of the property, and the farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain in the limited dry space. The herd consists of Florida Cracker cattle, a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. The cattle descend from animals brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s.

Residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders say other ranches and neighborhood properties have also flooded. They say water continued rising after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired the 315-acre Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. Residents continue to question the drainage system, as well as the source and volume of water flowing into the area.

The county said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on the breach affecting drainage into the irrigation canal. The agencies determined that repairs should wait until water levels recede because of safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee. The county’s immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions. It plans to make repairs when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. It is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County asks residents, businesses to report flood damage in survey
hero.body:
St. Lucie County is asking residents, businesses and agricultural property owners affected by recent flooding to report damage through an online survey to help officials assess the impacts and guide recovery efforts. Completing the survey is not an application for assistance and does not guarantee funding, county officials stressed.

The survey is open to property owners and tenants across the county, including Fort Pierce. Officials said the information collected will be shared with local, state and federal partners to document the extent of the flooding and help them understand the scope of the damage.

Respondents are asked to provide the property's location and building type, along with basic information about flooding and damage. The survey also asks about private wells used for household water and septic systems. Anyone with multiple affected structures should submit a separate survey for each one. The county is seeking reports about damage to buildings and their associated systems rather than flooding limited to yards or surrounding property.

Residents should report only conditions they have already observed. Officials warned people not to enter unsafe buildings, walk through floodwater or touch electrical equipment to assess damage.

Anyone who needs help completing the survey can contact the St. Lucie County Community Services Department at 772-462-1777 or comm_info@stlucieco.gov.

hero.headline: Two men arrested in Fort Pierce light pole theft during flooding emergency
hero.body:
Two South Florida men were arrested Friday after deputies said they stole about 34 aluminum light poles from a Fort Pierce property while St. Lucie County was under a flooding emergency. Both face burglary and grand theft charges tied to the state of emergency, according to the sheriff’s office.

Deputies and the South Florida Criminal Apprehension Team investigated suspicious activity Friday night at a property in the 3500 block of Eleven Mile Road. With help from the Fort Pierce Police Department, investigators used a drone to confirm that two people were removing property and loading it into a truck, the sheriff’s office said. Deputies tracked the truck as it left the area and stopped it on Okeechobee Road.

Pablo Rojas Castro, 33, of Pembroke Pines, and Alberto Guia Hernandez, 35, of Miami, were taken into custody without incident, according to the sheriff’s office. Investigators valued the stolen aluminum light poles at $6,800.

Castro and Hernandez face charges of burglary of an unoccupied dwelling during a state of emergency, traveling across county lines to commit burglary, grand theft during a state of emergency and possession of burglary tools. St. Lucie County remains under a state of emergency following this week’s flooding.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored with final salute at Saturday funeral
cards.teaser: Family, friends and fellow first responders honored the 34-year-old firefighter-paramedic, who died on duty Oct. 24 after nine years with the St. Lucie County Fire District.
cards.body:
Family, friends and fellow first responders gathered Saturday for the funeral of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, 34, who died on duty Oct. 24. An honor guard, a procession and firefighters standing side by side marked a final salute to his nine years of service with the St. Lucie County Fire District.

Hodge was remembered for his service to the community and the impact he had on those around him. “He was somebody who was always ready to help someone,” said his friend Jeff Lewis. “He leaves this place a better place than he found it. He found you one way but [would] leave you better than he found you.”

The St. Lucie County Fire District said Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to a hospital, where he later died.

His sister, Alexis Hodge, described the family's grief on Oct. 26. “It's a shock to literally all of us,” she said. She said one of the hardest parts was knowing she could no longer simply call her brother.

Hodge's death came about 15 months after the death of his brother, Jarius Hodge, who was also a firefighter. Jarius died in 2025.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary seeks temporary four-wheel-drive vehicles after flooding
hero.teaser: Save the Chimps needs taller vehicles after flooding disabled nearly 15 golf carts. Its more than 200 chimpanzees remain safe and continue receiving their normal care.
hero.body:
Save the Chimps in Fort Pierce is asking for temporary use of taller four-wheel-drive vehicles after flooding disabled nearly 15 golf carts used to move food, supplies and staff around the 150-acre sanctuary. The organization is seeking vehicles that can carry people and supplies while floodwaters remain.

The sanctuary’s more than 200 chimpanzees are safe and continue receiving their normal food, medication, enrichment and other daily care, according to Mark Yohannan, the organization’s director of facilities. He said the sanctuary received 19 inches of rain and is facing the worst flooding in its 25 years in Fort Pierce.

Since Tuesday, workers have used tractors and trailers to reach flooded areas and deliver supplies. Staff also used a drone to drop food to a chimpanzee during the flooding. Some employees have been unable to reach work, Yohannan said, while those who can get to the sanctuary have worked together to maintain care. “They're doing great. The care staff have been on their game,” he said. “They're getting everything they would get normally: enrichment, all their food, all their medication, blankets. They haven't missed a beat.”

The damaged golf carts normally support daily transportation across the property. “We'd seen the water and we figured, well, no big deal, we'll drive through it, and that became impossible immediately,” Yohannan said. The sanctuary is looking for taller four-wheel-drive vehicles that could be rented or donated for a short period. It is also asking the community for financial donations as staff work through the recovery. “A donation goes a long way,” he said.

Staff members are preparing to bring their concerns to the St. Lucie County Commission at a meeting next week. Yohannan also acknowledged that sanctuary employees and other Treasure Coast residents are dealing with flooding problems of their own. “There's a lot of people, including our own staff, that have much bigger problems with this water than we have here,” he said.

cards.headline: 11 arrested on racketeering charges in Fort Pierce gang investigation
cards.body:
Eleven people were arrested Wednesday on racketeering charges following an 18-month investigation into the 23rd Street Gang in Fort Pierce, according to the St. Lucie County sheriff’s office. Officials said two warrants remained outstanding.

Authorities called the investigation “Operation Scoreboard.” The sheriff’s office described the group as one of Fort Pierce’s most violent gangs and said it has ties to nearly 100 shootings.

Investigators said the 23rd Street Gang has between 70 and 80 documented members. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said members kept score of shootings and homicides.

“We took significant players off the streets yesterday, and there's more to come. There's more operations like this to come because we're not going to tolerate it here in St. Lucie County,” Del Toro said Thursday.

hero.headline: Deputies safely remove flood-displaced alligator from Indian River County driveway
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff's Office deputies safely removed an alligator from a residential driveway Friday after floodwaters pushed it out of its usual habitat. They relocated it to a more suitable area within the county. No one was hurt, and the alligator was unharmed.

Body camera video shows deputies approaching the alligator, which thrashed and hissed as they captured it before getting it into a caged van. The video also shows deputies releasing the animal back into the wild.

Recent flooding has displaced residents and wildlife, with animals appearing in unfamiliar areas. Alligators were confirmed in residential streets in Port St. Lucie on Thursday. An otter was also spotted after the flooding, and Martin County officials shared video of it navigating the changed landscape.

hero.headline: Indian River County floodwaters recede as crews drain roads and assess damage
hero.body:
Floodwaters are receding in Indian River County after this week’s severe downpours, with standing water still affecting some areas as crews work to drain roads and officials assess damage. County leaders said assessment teams were surveying damage Friday. Schools in Indian River County were closed Friday but are expected to reopen Monday.

Law enforcement officials said flooding reduced County Roads 510 and 512 to one lane at one point. Crews installed an emergency pipe under the roadway Thursday night to help drain the area. Officials are reminding residents to avoid flooded roads as cleanup continues.

Dave Kubacki, a resident of Sebastian, shared cellphone video of flooding outside his home and described how quickly the water receded. "Holy smoke, I can't believe how much water was out there, and I can't believe how fast it disappeared," Kubacki said. He said the only time flooding had been this bad was during a hurricane. "The hurricanes were bad, but I've never seen rain come down like this for such a long period of time and so heavy," he said.

Officials shared video of flooded roads taken just after the downpours, along with body camera footage showing deputies responding to incidents caused by high water. Deputies were called to a residential driveway to secure an alligator pushed out of its usual habitat by the flooding. The alligator was safely relocated to another area within the county.

hero.headline: Floodwater still fills Hyline Drive homes in Jensen Beach five days after historic rain
hero.body:
Residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach still face several feet of standing water inside their homes five days after historic rainfall flooded parts of the Treasure Coast. The street remains accessible only by boat or kayak, and the water is preventing residents from starting cleanup.

Floodwaters reach mailboxes and have entered most homes along the road. Longtime resident Linda Weisbecker said her home still has several feet of water inside, leaving decades of belongings and memories underwater.

“Sixty years of your life is gone. We raised our kids, our grandkids, our great-grandkids. It’s all gone,” Weisbecker said.

Her priority is getting the water out so she can begin cleaning up. “Our main goal is to get this water off so we can get in and start getting things done. If we don’t, it’s going to be that much worse,” she said.

Down the road, Lisa French said her home initially avoided flooding during Monday’s heavy rainfall. Water continued accumulating in the neighborhood and entered her home two days later. French, a stay-at-home mother whose household relies on a single income, is concerned about mold growth and how much of the home may need to be torn out and replaced. She said the standing water is keeping her family from beginning that work.

The neighborhood sits near the Savannas Preserve, where water can naturally flow south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. Martin County officials said crews will work to address flooding concerns and evaluate local watersheds to determine whether they have sufficient capacity to handle floodwaters.
