hero.headline: Trailside flooding crowds Hungryland Farms cattle onto high ground in Martin County
hero.body:
Flooding in Martin County’s Trailside community has forced Hungryland Farms’ cattle onto a narrow strip of higher ground, while repairs to a breach affecting drainage await lower water levels. Martin County said it and the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District determined that repairs should wait because of safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee.

Much of the farm’s pasture is underwater, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle on the elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico said. The flooding has cut off much of the property and left the herd with limited dry space. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. Other ranches and properties in the neighborhood have also flooded, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders, who say water continued rising after the rain stopped.

Residents and association leaders have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired the 315-acre Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. Its immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions, with repairs planned when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk.

The herd at Hungryland Farms belongs to a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. Florida Cracker cattle descend from cattle brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s and are valued for their connection to the state’s agricultural history.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County seeks flood-damage reports through Nov. 20 to guide recovery
hero.body:
St. Lucie County is asking residents, businesses and agricultural property owners affected by recent flooding to complete an online damage survey by Friday, Nov. 20. The survey will help officials document impacts to buildings and their associated systems and guide recovery efforts.

Completing the survey is not an application for assistance and does not guarantee that funding will be available, county officials said. The county will share the information with local, state and federal partners to help assess the extent of the flooding and better understand the scope of the damage.

The survey is open to property owners and tenants across the county. It asks for the property's location and building type, along with basic information about flooding and damage. Respondents also will be asked about private wells used for household water and septic systems.

Anyone with multiple affected structures should submit a separate survey for each one. The county is seeking reports of damage to buildings and their associated systems rather than flooding limited to yards or surrounding property.

Residents should report only conditions they have already observed. Officials warn people not to enter unsafe buildings, walk through floodwater or touch electrical equipment to assess damage.

Anyone who needs help completing the survey can contact the St. Lucie County Community Services Department at 772-462-1777 or comm_info@stlucieco.gov.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County residents affected by flooding can call for food assistance
cards.teaser: Residents needing meal resources can call 772-460-HELP (4357). The Sheriff’s Office is working with the Treasure Coast Food Bank and the county Emergency Operations Center.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County residents affected by recent flooding can call 772-460-HELP (4357) for food assistance. The Sheriff’s Office is working with the Treasure Coast Food Bank and the county Emergency Operations Center to connect residents with meal resources.

The food assistance line opens daily at 8 a.m. Residents who need meal resources because of the flooding can use that number, while emergencies requiring immediate assistance should be directed to 911.

Residents can also follow the Sheriff’s Office on social media for storm updates and other community information.

cards.headline: Flooding, equipment failures hamper care at Save the Chimps in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: Five days after heavy rain, staff can reach the sanctuary only by tractor, trailer or large off-road vehicle. The more than 200 rescued chimpanzees are safe, the sanctuary’s CEO said.
cards.body:
Floodwaters and equipment failures continue to hamper care at Save the Chimps in St. Lucie County five days after heavy rain flooded the region. Water still covers much of the 150-acre sanctuary, where employees can enter only by tractor, trailer or large off-road vehicle, according to the organization.

The sanctuary’s more than 200 rescued chimpanzees are safe, CEO Ana Paula Tavares said. They live on islands with care houses at higher elevations. Standing water across the property and surrounding area has made it difficult for staff to reach work and carry out their responsibilities. Save the Chimps said an overflowing local canal, Header Canal, has kept the floodwaters from receding.

A donated swamp buggy used by caregivers and veterinarians to travel around the sanctuary broke down Wednesday, the organization said. Golf carts used to transport food and supplies are also out of service after sitting in 1 to 2 feet of water. A staff member’s truck became stuck in a sinkhole near the sanctuary Thursday morning. The sanctuary said staff were delivering food to one chimp by drone.

Save the Chimps Facilities Director Mark Yohannan is scheduled to speak about the emergency at a North St. Lucie River Water District meeting at 10 a.m. at 14666 Orange Ave. The South Florida Water Management District issued an emergency order this week in response to flooding caused by heavy rain across several South Florida counties. Save the Chimps cares for chimpanzees rescued from research laboratories, the entertainment industry and the exotic pet trade.

hero.headline: Deputies remove flood-displaced alligator from Indian River County residential driveway
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff's Office deputies safely removed an alligator from a residential driveway Friday after floodwaters pushed it out of its usual habitat. No one was hurt, and the alligator was unharmed.

Body camera video shows deputies approaching the alligator, which thrashed and hissed as they captured it and placed it in a caged van. Deputies relocated the animal to a more suitable area within Indian River County. The video also shows them releasing it back into the wild.

Recent flooding has displaced residents and wildlife, bringing animals into unfamiliar areas. Alligators were confirmed in flooded residential streets in Port St. Lucie on Thursday. An otter was also spotted after the flooding, and Martin County officials shared video of it navigating the changed landscape.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County search-warrant operation includes two Fort Pierce homes
hero.body:
Law enforcement agencies carried out an operation involving five search warrants in St. Lucie County early Wednesday, with activity at two Fort Pierce homes. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed the operation was part of a large-scale criminal investigation involving the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

Law enforcement vehicles were seen at 1708 Miami Court and nearby at 1904 Georgia Avenue. Residents along Miami Court said loud explosions woke them during the operation. The sheriff's office said there was no known threat to the community.

“When you heard the sound, it sounded like a bomb; I thought, 'That's not a regular handgun, that sounds like a bomb,'” one neighbor said. She described a large law enforcement presence outside. “There were so many of them they were like a military. There was a military truck out there too,” she said.

The neighbor said she looked outside after the noises woke her and saw police lights. She watched as officers blocked off the road and issued commands over a loudspeaker.

hero.headline: Search warrants executed in St. Lucie County; residents urged to avoid active scenes
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office and the Fort Pierce Police Department carried out several search warrants Wednesday morning as part of a criminal investigation in the region. The operation involved personnel from both agencies, with the sheriff’s office advising residents that they could notice more law enforcement officers in some areas while the work continued. Authorities asked people to stay away from places where officers were actively working and to follow instructions from personnel at those scenes. The sheriff’s office also said the operation posed no threat to the community.

During the operation, Fort Pierce police officers arrested a woman and put her in a police car. The arrest took place as law enforcement agencies were carrying out the search warrants Wednesday morning. Fort Pierce police were working with the sheriff’s office on the broader operation, which involved multiple warrants connected to a criminal investigation. Along with the arrest, the activity prompted a notice to residents about the police presence they might encounter. That notice asked the public to give officers room to work by avoiding locations where law enforcement activity was taking place.

The sheriff’s office advised residents that an increased law enforcement presence could remain visible in some areas as the operation continued. Its guidance was to avoid active scenes and comply with directions given by personnel there. For people who encountered officers working in their area, the agency’s request was the same: stay away from the activity and follow instructions at the scene. The advisory concerned the ongoing search-warrant operation involving the sheriff’s office and Fort Pierce police. Authorities paired that request for the public’s cooperation with an assurance that there was no threat to the community.

The multiple search warrants, the woman’s arrest and the public advisory were all part of Wednesday morning’s law enforcement activity in St. Lucie County. The sheriff’s office described the searches as part of a criminal investigation and said its personnel were collaborating with Fort Pierce police. As that work continued, residents were urged to remain clear of active law enforcement locations rather than approach the scenes. The agency’s message distinguished the visible police activity from a community threat: residents might see additional officers in some areas, but the sheriff’s office said the public was not in danger from the operation.
